From al-Thawri: Whoever claims that he is truly a believer in Allah, but does not testify that he is among the people of Paradise, has believed in half of the verse. This is an argument against him: just as he does not affirm with certainty that he is among those who merit the reward of true believers, so he does not affirm with certainty that he is a true believer. By this, those who make an exception (*istithnāʾ*) in faith hold on. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, was among those who did not make an exception in it. It is related from him that he said to Qatada: "Why do you make an exception in your faith?" He said: "Following Abraham, peace be upon him, in his words, *wa-alladhī aṭmaʿu an yaghfira lī khaṭīʾatī yawma al-dīn* ("and who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgement")." He said to him: "Why did you not follow him in his words, *awa-lam tu'min? Qāla balā* ("Have you not believed? He said: Yes")?"

*Darajāt* ("degrees"): nobility, honour, exaltedness of rank. *Wa-maghfira* ("and forgiveness"): pardon and overlooking of their misdeeds. *Wa-rizqun karīm* ("and generous provision"): the bliss of Paradise, meaning for them are good, lasting benefits by way of honour; and this is the meaning of reward.

As your Lord brought you out ﴿كَمَا أَخْرَجَكَ رَبُّكَ﴾ has two interpretations.

[[Mahmud said: "Regarding *kama* (as, just as) there are two interpretations. The first: the place of the *kaf* is in the nominative case..." etc.]] Ahmad said: My grandfather Abu al-Abbas Ahmad al-Faqih al-Wazir, may Allah have mercy on him, used to mention for the meaning of the verse a third interpretation, superior to these two. It is that the intended meaning is to liken the Prophet's (ﷺ) distinction regarding the spoils (*anfal*), and the entrusting of their matter to his judgment with respect to reward and recompense, to his bringing out from his house obeying Allah, the Exalted, listening to His command and content with His decree, despite the believers' dislike of this in obedience. So Allah likened His reward for this distinction to the pleasing obedience of the Prophet (ﷺ). Just as his obedience reached the utmost degree among kinds of obedience, so Allah's recompense to him reached the utmost degree among kinds of rewards. The sum of this meaning is what the Prophet (ﷺ) alluded to when he said: "The reward is according to the hardship." For this meaning you may also make the *kaf* nominative or accusative, according to the grammatical estimation. And Allah is the Granter of success.

The first: the place of the *kaf* is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimate is: "This situation is like the situation of your bringing out." That is, their condition in disliking what you saw of the giving of spoils to the raiders is like their condition in disliking your going out to war.

The second: it is accusative, as an adjectival qualifier (*sifah*) of a verbal noun of the verb estimated in His saying ﴿The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾; that is, the spoils were established for Allah and the Messenger and confirmed, despite their dislike, with a confirmation like the confirmation of your Lord's bringing you out of your house while they were averse.

"From your house" means his house in Medina, or Medina itself, because it was his emigration place and dwelling; so its being specific to him is like the house's being specific to its occupant. ﴿In truth﴾ means a bringing out accompanied by wisdom and rightness from which there is no escape. ﴿And indeed a group of the believers were averse﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: He brought you out while they were averse.

This is because the caravan of Quraysh came from Syria, carrying great trade, with forty riders, among them Abu Sufyan, Amr ibn al-As, and Amr ibn Hisham. [[This story is taken from the *Sirah* (the biography of the Prophet) of Ibn Hisham, except his saying "among the people of the caravan was Amr ibn Hisham," for Amr ibn Hisham is Abu Jahl, and he was not in the caravan but in the army that marched out (*nafir*). Al-Tabari reported it from the words of Ibn Ishaq, part of it from Ibn Abbas, from Urwah, and from al-Suddi, with changes of order, additions and omissions. In the *Maghazi* of al-Waqidi it is reported from Mahmud ibn Labid in part, and from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib in part.]] Gabriel informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he informed the Muslims. They were pleased to intercept the caravan because of its abundant wealth and the people's small number. When they set out, the news of their departure reached the people of Mecca. Abu Jahl called out from atop the Ka'bah: "O people of Mecca, to the rescue, to the rescue! On every swift and slow mount! Your caravan, your wealth! If Muhammad seizes it, you will never prosper after this!" The sister of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib had seen a dream and said to her brother: "I saw a wondrous thing: it was as if a king descended from the sky, took a rock from the mountain, and flung it, and no house in Mecca remained without being struck by a stone from that rock." Al-Abbas related it, and Abu Jahl said: "Their men are not content to have prophets until their women prophesy!" Abu Jahl set out with all the people of Mecca, and they were the army (*nafir*). Hence the proverb: "Neither with the caravan nor with the army" (*la fi al-ʿayr wa la fi al-nafir*).

It was said to him: "The caravan has taken the coastal road and escaped, so return with the people to Mecca." He said: "No, by Allah, that will never happen until we slaughter camels, drink wine, and have singing girls and musical instruments at Badr, so that all the Arabs will hear of our march. Muhammad did not get the caravan, and we have bitten him." [[His saying "and we have bitten him" (*a'dadnahu*): in *al-Sihah* (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), *a'dadtuhu al-shay'a fa'addahu* means I made him bite the thing. And in the hadith: "bite him with the penis of his father" (*fa-a'dhuhu bi-hinna abihi*)... one says *a'dadtuhu sayfi*, meaning I struck him with it. *A'idha al-qawm* means the people's camels ate *al-ʿadd*, which with a *damma* is fodder of the cities, and with a *kasra* is small thorn.]] He went on with them to Badr, and Badr was a water where the Arabs used to gather for their market one day a year. Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended and said: "O Muhammad, Allah has promised you one of the two groups: either the caravan or Quraysh." The Prophet (ﷺ) consulted his companions and said: "What do you say? The people have set out from Mecca on every swift and slow mount. Do you prefer the caravan over the army?" They said: "Rather, the caravan is more beloved to us than meeting the enemy." The face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) changed. Then he repeated to them and said: "The caravan has passed along the sea coast, and this is Abu Jahl coming." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, take the caravan and leave the enemy." Then, at the anger of the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, stood and spoke well. Then Sa'd ibn Ubadah stood and said: "Proceed with your matter. By Allah, if you were to journey to Aden Abyan [[His saying "Aden Abyan": in *al-Sihah*, Abyan is the name of a man to whom Aden is attributed, so it is said Aden Abyan. (Ea)]], not a man of the Ansar would stay behind from you." Then al-Miqdad ibn Amr said: "O Messenger of Allah, go forward with what Allah has commanded you, for we are with you wherever you wish. We will not say to you what the children of Israel said to Musa: 'Go you and your Lord and fight; we are sitting here.' Rather: 'Go you and your Lord and fight; we are fighting with you both,' as long as one eye of ours blinks." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed, then said: "Advise me, O people," meaning the Ansar, because they had said to him when they pledged allegiance to him at the Aqabah: "We are free of our covenant with you until you reach our dwellings. When you arrive among us, you are under our protection; we will protect you from what we protect our fathers and women from." The Prophet (ﷺ) feared that the Ansar would not consider it their duty to support him except against an enemy who attacked them in Medina. [[His saying "feared that the Ansar would not consider": perhaps it is "that they would be" or perhaps "the Ansar consider"; in any case, one of the two particles suffices for the other. (Ea)]]

Then Sa'd ibn Mu'adh stood and said: "As if you mean us, O Messenger of Allah?"

He said: "Yes."

He said: "We have believed in you and affirmed you, and we testified that what you brought is the truth, and we gave you on that our covenants and pledges to hear and obey. So proceed, O Messenger of Allah, with what you desire. By He who sent you with the truth, if you were to lead us into this sea and plunge into it, we would plunge with you; not one man of us would stay behind. We do not dislike that you meet our enemy with us. We are patient in war and truthful at the encounter. Perhaps Allah will show you from us what will delight your eye. So march with us in Allah's blessing."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoiced, and Sa'd's words pleased him. Then he said: "Proceed in Allah's blessing and rejoice, for Allah has promised me one of the two groups, and by Allah, I now see the places where the people will fall."

It is related that it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he finished at Badr: "Pursue the caravan, nothing stands between you and it." Al-Abbas called out to him while he was in bonds: "It is not fitting!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Why?"

He said: "Because Allah promised you one of the two groups, and He has given you what He promised you."

[[Al-Tirmidhi, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Ya'la, al-Bazzar, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim narrated it from the narration of Isra'il from Simak from Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]

The aversion was from some of them, due to His saying ﴿And indeed a group of the believers were averse﴾.

The truth about which they argued with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was: [their disliking] to meet the armed troop (al-nafir), because they preferred to meet the caravan (al-ʿir), after it had become clear, following the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) announcement, that they would be granted victory. Their argument was their saying: "We did not set out except for the caravan; why did you not tell us, so that we could prepare and get ready?" This was because of their aversion to fighting. Then He likened their state, in their extreme alarm and terror as they were being led toward victory and booty, to the state of one who is dragged to be killed [[His saying "like one who is dragged to killing" means: he is pulled with great force. Cited from al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] and driven in humiliation to certain death, while he witnesses its causes, looks at them, and has no doubt about them.

It has been said: their fear was due to the small number [of their men], and that they were infantry. It is also narrated that there were only two horsemen among them.

Translation:

"Idh" is in the accusative, governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember). "Anna-ha lakum" ("that it is for you") is a substitution (badal) for "iḥdā al-ṭā'ifatayn" (one of the two groups). The two groups are: the caravan (al-ʿīr) and the army (al-nafīr).

"Ghayra dhāti al-shawka" (not the one with the thorn/might): the caravan, because there were only forty horsemen in it, while the might (al-shawka) lay with the army, by virtue of their number and equipment. Al-shawka means sharpness (ḥidda), used figuratively from the word for a thorn (shawk). It is said: "shawk al-qanā" for the points of the spear (shibāhā). From this come the expressions "shā'ik al-silāh" (one whose weapons are sharp). That is, you wished that the caravan would be yours, because it is the group that has no sharpness or strength, and you did not want the other group. "An yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq" (that He would establish the truth): that He would confirm and exalt it "bi-kalimātihi" (by His words), that is, by His verses revealed concerning the fighting of the one with might, and by what He commanded of the angels regarding their descent to give victory, and by what He decreed concerning their capture, killing, and throwing into the well of Badr.

"Al-dābir al-ākhir" is an active participle from dabara, when it turns its back. From it comes "dābirat al-ṭā'ir" (the bird's rear). "Qaṭʿ al-dābir" is an expression for total eradication (istiʾṣāl). The meaning is that you desire the immediate benefit and the trivial matters, "wa-an lā talqū mā yarzu'ukum fī abdānikum wa-aḥwālikum" (and that you would not meet what harms you in your bodies and your conditions), while God, Mighty and Majestic, desires the lofty matters, and what returns to the establishment of the religion, the victory of the truth, the exaltation of the Word, and success in both abodes. "Shatān mā bayna al-muradayn" (how far apart are the two desires). That is why He chose for you the group with might, broke their strength through your weakness, overcame their multitude through your fewness, and honored you and humbled them, and granted you what the caravan and what is in it could not match even at its lowest.

"Wa-quriʾa: bi-kalimatihi," read in the singular (al-tawḥīd).

Ask: with what does His saying ﴿li-yuhiqqa al-haqqa﴾ (so that He might establish the truth) connect? I say: with an omitted element whose estimated form is: "so that He might establish the truth and nullify the falsehood, He did that, and did not do it except for these two purposes." And these are: establishing Islam and making it manifest, and nullifying disbelief and erasing it.

If you ask: Isn't this a repetition? I say: No, because the two meanings are distinct. The first (clause) is a distinction between the two wishes, whereas this one is a statement of His purpose in what He did, namely choosing the one with the might (dhat al-shawkah) over others for them, and granting them victory over it, and that He did not give them victory nor abandon those others except for this purpose, which is the lord of purposes. The omitted element must be estimated as postponed so that it conveys the meaning of exclusivity (ikhtisas), and the meaning fits it. It was also said: it is connected with "yaqta'a" (to cut off).

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 9:**

If you ask, "What does ﴿إِذْ تَسْتَغِيثُونَ﴾ (when you were seeking help) depend on?" I say: it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿إِذْ يَعِدُكُمُ﴾ (when He promised you). It has also been said that it depends on His words ﴿لِيُحِقَّ الْحَقَّ وَيُبْطِلَ الْبَاطِلَ﴾ (to establish the truth and nullify falsehood). Their seeking help consisted of this: when they knew that fighting was unavoidable, they began calling upon Allah and saying, "Our Lord, give us victory over Your enemy, O Helper of those who seek help, help us." It is reported from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the polytheists, who were a thousand, and at his companions, who were three hundred. He turned to the qibla, stretched out his hands, and supplicated: "O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O Allah, if this band perishes, You will not be worshipped on the earth." He kept on like this until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, picked it up, placed it on his shoulder, embraced him from behind, and said, "O Prophet of Allah, your pleading with your Lord is enough, for He will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you." [[Recorded by Muslim from the narration of Ibn Abbas on the authority of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

﴿أَنِّي مُمِدُّكُمْ﴾ (that I will reinforce you): its original form is ﴿بِأَنِّي مُمِدُّكُمْ﴾ (with the fact that I will reinforce you). The preposition was dropped and the verb ﴿اسْتَجَابَ﴾ (responded) governed it, so its place was in the accusative case. It is reported from Abu Amr that he recited ﴿أَنِّي مُمِدُّكُمْ﴾ with a kasra (إِنِّي), either intending a verb of saying, or treating ﴿اسْتَجَابَ﴾ as if it were ﴿قَالَ﴾ (he said), because responding is a kind of speech.

If you ask, "Did the angels fight on the day of Badr?" I say: this is disputed. It has been said that Gabriel descended on the day of Badr with five hundred angels on the right wing, where Abu Bakr was, and Michael with five hundred on the left wing, where Ali ibn Abi Talib was, in the forms of men, wearing white garments and white turbans, with the ends of the turbans hanging down between their shoulders. It was also said that they fought on the day of Badr but did not fight on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) or on the day of Hunayn.

It is reported that Abu Jahl said to Ibn Mas'ud, "Where did that voice come from which we used to hear without seeing any figure?" He said, "From the angels." Abu Jahl said, "They defeated us, not you." It is also related that a man from the Muslims, while running after a man from the polytheists, heard the sound of a whip-blow above him, and then looked and saw the polytheist fall flat on his back with his face split. The Ansari told the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said, "You have spoken the truth; that was reinforcement from the heavens." [[This is part of a hadith from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, the one mentioned before it.]]

It is also reported from Abu Dawud al-Mazini: "I pursued a man from the polytheists to strike him on the day of Badr, but his head fell before my sword reached him." [[Recorded by Ibn Ishaq in al-Maghazi: "My father related to me from men of Banu Mazin, from Abu Dawud al-Mazini," and so on; it was also recorded through his chain by Ishaq, al-Tabari, and others.]]

It has also been said that they did not fight; they only increased the numbers and strengthened the believers. Otherwise, one angel is enough to destroy all the people of the world, for Gabriel, peace be upon him, destroyed the cities of the people of Lot with a feather from his wing, and destroyed the land of Thamud, the people of Salih, with a single cry.

﴿مُرْدِفِينَ﴾ (following one after another) is recited with a kasra and with a fatha on the dal, from your saying "radifahu," meaning he followed him. From the same root is His saying ﴿رَدِفَ لَكُمْ بَعْضُ الَّذِي تَسْتَعْجِلُونَ﴾ (some of what you were hastening for has come close behind you), meaning it followed you. "Ardafatuhu iyyah" means I made him follow it. It is also said "ardaftuhu," like "atba'tuhu" (I made him follow), when you come after him. So the form with a kasra on the dal must mean either "following" (mut'abi'in), or "making follow" (mut'ibin). If it means "following," it must mean either: following one another; or following one another for others; or following them, the believers, that is, they go before them and then follow them themselves; or following them as escorts, sending them forward before them while they remain at their rear, so that they are under their watch and protection; or following themselves, other angels; or following other angels. This last view is supported by His saying in the surah of Al 'Imran: ﴿بِثَلَاثَةِ آلَافٍ مِنَ الْمَلَائِكَةِ مُنْزَلِينَ﴾ (with three thousand angels sent down) and ﴿بِخَمْسَةِ آلَافٍ مِنَ الْمَلَائِكَةِ مُسَوِّمِينَ﴾ (with five thousand angels marked). Whoever recites ﴿مُرْدِفِينَ﴾ with a fatha means "following" or "made to follow."

It is also recited ﴿مُرَدِّفِينَ﴾ (mu radrdifin) with a kasra or a damma on the ra and a shaddah on the dal. Its original form is ﴿مُرْتَدِفِينَ﴾ (mirtadifin), meaning "successively following" or "following," from "irtadafahu." The ta of the infix was assimilated into the dal, and two consecutive unvowelled consonants met, so the ra was given a kasra according to the original form, or a kasra to match the dal, or a damma to match the mim.

It is reported from al-Suddi: ﴿بِآلَافٍ مِنَ الْمَلَائِكَةِ﴾ (with thousands of angels), in the plural, to agree with what is in the surah of Al 'Imran.

If you ask, "How then is the one who recited it in the singular excused, and who did not explain ﴿الْمُرْدِفِينَ﴾ as the angels making other angels follow them, or as the following ones following others?" I say: the meaning of "the thousand" is those among them who fought, or the leaders among them, and those other than them are their followers.

Translation:

If you ask: to what does the pronoun in "wa-ma ja'alahu" refer? I answer: to His saying "anni mumiddukum" (that I am reinforcing you), because the meaning is: "So He answered you by reinforcing you."

If you ask: what about the one who reads it with kasra (inna, "indeed")? I answer: it refers to His saying "anni mumiddukum," since it is the object of an implied verb of saying, so it carries the meaning of a saying.

It is also permissible that it refers to the reinforcement (al-imdad) which is indicated by "mumiddukum": "And Allah did not make it except as glad tidings (illa bushra), that is, as good news to you of victory, like the tranquility (al-sakina) given to the Children of Israel." He means: you sought aid and humbled yourselves before Allah because of your small number and weakness, so the reinforcement by the angels was good news to you of victory, and a calming for you, and a steadying of your hearts. "And victory is not from anyone but Allah" (﴿وَمَا النَّصْرُ إِلَّا مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾): he means, do not suppose that victory comes from the angels, for the one who gives victory is Allah, to you and to the angels. Or: "And victory is not from the angels or other means except from Allah," and the one who is victorious is the one whom Allah has given victory.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 11:

إِذْ يُغَشِّيكُمُ (idh yughashshikum) is a second substitute (badal thani) for إِذْ يَعِدُكُمُ (idh ya'idukum), or it is in the accusative case governed by النصر (al-nasr), or by what is implied in مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ (min 'indi Allah) of the sense of a verb, or by what Allah has made (ja'alahu Allah), or by an implied اذكر (udhkur, "remember"). It is also read يغشيكم (yughshikum) with the lightened and the doubled form.

[[Mahmud said: "And it is read إِذْ يُغَشِّيكُمُ with lightening and doubling... etc." Ahmad said: A similar consideration applies at the saying of the Exalted, هُوَ الَّذِي يُرِيكُمُ الْبَرْقَ خَوْفاً وَطَمَعاً (It is He who shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope), because the agent of the seeing is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the agent of the fear and hope is they, and both have been put in the accusative as objects of purpose (maf'ulan lahuma). The answer is: since when Allah shows them the lightning they see it, they were agents in meaning, and the meaning was "He it is who shows you the lightning, so you see it, as fear and as hope." So this is like the verse of al-Anfal, for the object in meaning is the agent. There will be further discussion of this point. The pen has hastened to address it here, because one might say: the agent of the covering by sleep (al-nu'as) over them is Allah the Exalted, and He is also the agent of the security (al-amanah) and its creator; then the agent of the act and the cause become one, the question is removed, and the difficulty disappears according to the principles of the Sunnah which require attributing the acts of creatures to Allah as their creator and originator. The questioner may say: what is required is that the agent of the act be qualified by the cause as he is qualified by the act; and if the Creator of security is the servant, and the servant is secure by it, then the servant is the linguistic agent, whereas if Allah is the agent in reality and in belief, then the question returns to the earlier answer. And Allah is the Granter of success.]] The noun al-nu'as (النعاس, sleep/drowsiness) and the pronoun are in the accusative, referring to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. أَمَنَةً (amanatan, "security") is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). If you say: must the agent of the caused act and the cause not be one? I say: Yes, but since the meaning of يغشاكم النعاس (yaghshakumu al-nu'as) is "you become drowsy" (tan'asun), amanatan is put in the accusative on the basis that the sleep and the security belong to them. The meaning is: "when you become drowsy in security," i.e., "as security," meaning "for your security," and مِنْهُ (minhu, "from Him") is a description of it: that is, a security obtained by you from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If you say: then on other than this reading? I say: it is permissible for amanatan to mean faith (iman), i.e., He makes you drowsy with faith from Him; or [it is in the sense of] "He covers you with sleep so that you become drowsy in security." If you say: is it permissible that it be in the accusative on the basis that the security belongs to the sleep which is the agent of yaghshakum? That is, "the sleep covers you because of its security," the attribution of security to sleep being figurative, while it truly belongs to the people of sleep; or [it means] that He made you sleep at a time when, in such a frightening situation, sleep should by right not have dared to overcome you, and it overcame you only as a security obtained from Allah, which without it would not have covered you, in the manner of personification and imagery? I say: the eloquence of the Qur'an is not far from admitting this, and it has parallels in it, and one who said the following alluded to it:

يهاب النّوم أن يغشى عيونا ... تهابك فهو نفّار شرود
Sleep fears to cover eyes... they fear you, so it is skittish and wandering.

[[By al-Zamakhshari. He means: sleep shrinks from covering eyes that fear you, so sleep is very skittish and wandering. He likened it to an animal that can be described as fearing, by way of metaphor (al-makniyya). His saying "so it is skittish and wandering" is a consequential elaboration (tafri' lil-tarshih). And the attribution of fear to the eyes is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli).]]

It is also read أَمَنَةً (amanah) with the sukun on the mim. Its parallel is أَمِنَ أَمَنَةً (amina amanatan) like حَيِيَ حَيَاةً (hayiya hayatan), and like أَمِنَ أَمَنَةً (amina amanatan) like رَحِمَ رَحْمَةً (rahima rahmatan). The meaning: the fear that was upon them would have prevented them from sleeping; so when Allah calmed their hearts and made them secure, they slept. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Drowsiness in battle is security from Allah, and in prayer it is a whisper from Satan."

[[I have not found it from Ibn 'Abbas. The apparent thing is that it is a distortion, and it is actually Ibn Mas'ud. Thus al-Tha'labi mentioned it. It was narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabari, and similarly Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tabarani, all from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud as a mawquf report.]]

وَيُنَزِّلُ (wa yunazzilu, "and He sends down") is read with the lightened and the heavy form. Al-Sha'bi read: مَا لِيُطَهِّرَكُمْ بِهِ (ma li-yutahhirakum bihi, "to purify you by it"). Ibn Jinni said: مَا (ma) is a relative pronoun, and its relative clause is the prepositional phrase governed by the preposition, so it is as if he said: "what is for purification."

رِجْزَ الشَّيْطَانِ (rijza al-shaytan, "the defilement of Satan") is his whispering to them and his frightening them with thirst. It was also said: it is ritual impurity (janabah), because it is of his imagining.

It is read: رِجْسَ الشَّيْطَانِ (rijsa al-shaytan) ...

That is because Iblis appeared to them, while the polytheists had preceded them to the water. [[Al-Tha'labi without a chain. It was narrated by al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh through the route of 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas at length, and in this there is what is not in the other; it is in Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi's Dala'il from this route.]] The Muslims descended upon a reddish sand dune in which feet sank, without water, and they slept, and most of them had wet dreams. He said to them: "You, companions of Muhammad, claim that you are upon the truth and that you pray without ablution and in a state of major impurity, and you are thirsty. If you were upon truth, these people would not have overcome you at the water, and they are only waiting for thirst to exhaust you; when thirst cuts your necks, they will walk to you and kill whom they love and drive the rest of you to Mecca." They grieved greatly and were apprehensive. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, sent down rain; it rained at night until the valley flowed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions made basins on the side of the valley, watered the mounts, bathed and performed ablution. The sand that had been between them and the enemy became firm, so that feet could stand on it, the whispering of Satan departed, and hearts were content. The pronoun in بِهِ (bihi) refers to the water. It is also permissible that it refers to the binding (al-rabt), because when patience and boldness are firmly established in the heart, the foot stands firm in the places of battle.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 12:

﴿When your Lord inspired the angels﴾ may be a third substitute (badal) for ﴿when He promised you﴾, and it may be that ﴿Make firm﴾ governs it. ﴿That I am with you﴾ is the object of ﴿inspired﴾. It is also read as ﴿Innī﴾ with a kasra, either by intending a saying (qawl), or by treating ﴿inspired﴾ as if it were ﴿says﴾, as in His words ﴿That I am sending you reinforcements﴾. The meaning is: "I am your helper in making them firm, so make them firm." His words ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike﴾ may be an explanation of His words ﴿that I am with you, so make firm﴾. There is no greater help than casting terror into the hearts of the disbelievers, and no more effective firming than striking their necks. The two together are the utmost victory.

It may also be something other than an explanation: "making firm" may mean that they bring to mind what strengthens their hearts, what makes their resolve and intentions sound in fighting, and that they show what makes them certain that they are being reinforced by the angels. It was said: the angel would take the appearance of a man whom they knew by face, come to them and say, "I have heard the polytheists saying, 'By God, if they charge against us, we will be routed,'" and he would walk between the two lines saying, "Rejoice, for God is your helper, because you worship Him and these do not worship Him."

It is read as ﴿the terror﴾ with the doubled letter (tathqil). ﴿Above the necks﴾ means the upper parts of the necks, which are the places of slaughter, since they are joints; so striking there is a cutting and the flying off of heads. It was also said that it means the heads, since they are above the necks, meaning striking the skulls. He said:

*"And I strike the skull of the hero who is fierce."* [[The explanation of this witness was given in the first volume, page 409, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

*"I overtook him while he was in a dense, fearless mass,*
*with a sharp sword that struck the middle of the head and split it."*

*"A horseman plunged into the surges of death,*
*when he swore an oath upon a hateful matter, and he spoke truly."*

*"I overtook him while he was in a dense, fearless mass,*
*with a sharp sword that struck the middle of the head and split it."*

This is said of the dishonest... (the poet, of the Banu Qays al-Kinani). "The surge" (al-ghamr) is abundant water, so he likens death to a great flood by way of metonymy (kināya). "Plunging into it" (al-ghimar wa'l-inghimas) is an imagining (takhyīl).

It is permissible that "the surge" (al-ghimar) be used as a metaphor (isti'āra) for the horrors of death in the explicit form (taṣrīḥiyya). It may also be used as an explicit metaphor for that horseman's army. He attributed it to death because it arises from it, and "plunging" is a supporting detail (tarshīḥ). "When he swore" means he swore. "Upon a hateful matter" means war. "Spoke truly" means he was righteous in his oath. "I overtook him" means I reached him, while he was "in a dense mass" meaning a great battalion that had turned black or green with the abundance of weapons and armour, from *al-jawa* like *al-hawa*, or from *al-ju'wa* like *al-humra*, and it is the same, on condition that blackness covers it. It was said that the blackness is overlaid with greenness from the rust of its armour. "Fearless" means preventing and stern. It is also permissible that *al-ja'wā'* means rusty armour. "A sharp sword" is the object of "I overtook him", meaning a cutting sword. "Struck" means sought and attained. "The middle" means the middle of the head. "Split" means the head or its middle split. He praised his opponent together with his own triumph over him, to show that he reached the utmost courage.

"The fingertips" (al-banān) are the fingers, and he means their extremities. The meaning is: strike the vital places and the extremities, since a blow either lands on a deadly spot or on a non-deadly one, so He commanded them to combine both types together.

It is also permissible that His words ﴿I will cast﴾ up to His words ﴿every fingertip﴾, following His words ﴿so make firm those who believed﴾, be an instruction to the angels about what they should use to make them firm, as if He said, "Tell them the words ﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾", or as if they had said, "How shall we make them firm?" Then it was said, "Tell them the words ﴿I will cast﴾." On this view, the ones who strike are the believers.

This refers to what befell them of striking, killing, and immediate punishment. It is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada') of a sentence, and *annahum* (that they) is its predicate (khabar). The meaning is that this punishment fell upon them because of their opposition (mushaqqah).

Mushaqqah is derived from *shaqq* (split), because each of the two opponents is on a side opposite to the other's side. I was once asked in a dream about the derivation of *mu'adah* (enmity), and I said: because this one is on one edge (*'idwah*) and that one is on the other edge, just as it is said of *al-mukhasamah* and *al-mushaqqah*: because this one is in one *khasm* (side), and that one is in the other *khasm*, and this one is in one *shiqq* (side), and that one is in the other *shiqq*.

The *kaf* in *dhalika* is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to each individual listener. The *kaf* in *dhalikum* is addressed to the disbelievers, in the manner of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical address). The position of *dhalikum* is nominative, meaning "that punishment," or "the punishment is that," or it may be in the accusative, meaning "upon you is that," so *fadhuquhu* (then taste it), like your saying: "Zaydan, so strike him."

﴿Wa-anna lil-kafirina﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with *dhalikum* in both of its grammatical readings, or it may be in the accusative on the basis that the *waw* means "together with." The meaning is: taste this immediate punishment together with the deferred punishment that awaits you in the Hereafter. Thus the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun.

Al-Hasan recited *wa-inna* with a kasra.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verses 15–16:

زَحْفاً (zahfan) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from alladhīna kafarū. Al-zaḥf (the advancing host) is the great army (al-jaysh al-dahm) [[His phrase "al-jaysh al-dahm" means a large number; al-dahmah means blackness, as in the Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿA.)]] which, because of its numbers, appears as if it is creeping forward, i.e., advancing step by step, from zaḥafa al-ṣabī (the child's crawling) when he crawls on his buttocks little by little. It is named by the verbal noun, and its plural is zuḥūf. The meaning is: when you meet them in battle while they are numerous and vast and you are few, do not flee, let alone that you should approach them in number or equal them. Or it is a circumstantial accusative from both groups, meaning: when you meet them while both they and you are advancing toward each other. Or it is a circumstantial accusative from the believers, as if they were made aware of what would happen from them on the day of Ḥunayn when they turned their backs in retreat, and they were a host of the hosts of twelve thousand, and it is a warning [[His phrase "wa-taqaddumah nahy lahum" is perhaps coordinated on the meaning, i.e., ishʿāran wa-taqaddumah nahy. (ʿA.)]] and a preliminary prohibition to them against fleeing on that day. And in His saying, "and whoever turns his back to them on that day," there is an indication of this, except one who swerves for battle (mutaḥarrifan li-qitāl), which is the counterattack after the feigned flight, when the enemy imagines that he has been defeated and then he turns upon him; and this is a category of the stratagems and deceptions of war. Or one who withdraws to a company (mutaḥayyizan aw munḥāzan ilā fiʾah), that is, to another group of Muslims other than the company in which he is.

It is related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "A detachment set out and I was among them, and they fled. When they returned to Medina they felt ashamed and entered the houses. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we are the fugitives.' He said: 'Rather, you are the returners (al-ʿakkārūn) [[His phrase "al-ʿakkārūn" comes from ʿakara, meaning to turn back and charge again. Reported by the Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿA.)]] and I am your company (fiʾah).'" And a man fled from al-Qādisiyyah, then came to Medina to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, and said:

"O Commander of the Faithful, I am ruined; I fled from the advancing host." ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I am your company" [[Reported by Ibn Abi Shaybah through the narration of Manṣūr from Ibrāhīm. He said: "A man fled," and he mentioned it.]]. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him: "Fleeing from the advancing host is among the greatest of the major sins."

If you say: With what is illā mutaḥarrifan in the accusative case?

I say: It is a circumstantial accusative, and otherwise illā is superfluous (laghw). Or it is an exception from the ones who turn back, meaning: "and whoever turns his back to them, except a man among them who swerves or withdraws." Al-Ḥasan read duburahu with a sukun, and the pattern of mutaḥayyiz is mutafayyil, not mutafaʿʿil, because it derives from ḥāza yaḥūz, so the form of the derived verb from it is mutaḥawwiz.

When the two hosts met, he said to Ali (may God be pleased with him), "Give me a handful of pebbles from the valley," and he threw them into their faces and said, "May the faces be disfigured." They fled, and the believers pursued them, killing and taking them prisoner.[[Al-Tibi said: None of the imams of hadith has mentioned that this throwing took place at Badr. Then the Muslims pursued them, killing and taking them prisoner. And God sent down: ﴿So you did not kill them, but God killed them﴾, the verse. Not one of them remained without his face and eyes filled, and the enemies of God fled while the Muslims killed and took prisoners." Al-Tabari also narrated it by another route from Hakim ibn Hizam, similar to it, except for what is at its end.]] So it was said to them: ﴿So you did not kill them﴾. The "fa" (then) is the answer to an implied condition, its sense being: if you boast of killing them, then you did not kill them. ﴿But God killed them﴾, because it is He who sent down the angels, cast terror into their hearts, decreed victory and triumph, strengthened your hearts, and removed from them fear and dread. ﴿And you did not throw, Muhammad, when you threw, but God threw.﴾ The meaning is that the throw you threw was not truly thrown by you, for if you had thrown it, its effect would not have reached beyond what the throw of a human reaches. Rather, it was the throw of God, since it produced that great effect. So the throwing was attributed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) because its outward form came from him, and it was denied of him because its effect, which no human can bear, is the act of God, Mighty and Majestic. Thus God is in truth the doer of the throw, as if it had never existed from the Messenger (peace be upon him) at all. It was also read: "But God killed them" and "But God threw," with "lakinna" lightened and what follows it in the nominative. ﴿And that He might bestow upon the believers a good bestowal﴾, that is, He might give them a fine gift. Zuhayr said:

*"May God reward with goodness what the two of them did for you,
and may He bestow upon them the best of bestowals, which is the bestowing."*

He means: God repays their kindness toward you with His own kindness. Abla here carries the meaning of "to give." One says: "Allah balahu and abla'hu and ibtala'" meaning "He tested him." The noun is *bala'*. It may mean a calamity, and it may mean a blessing, as here. He gave them the best of His blessing, by which people are tested and examined. The meaning is: for the goodness toward the believers He did what He did, and He did it only for that. ﴿Indeed God is Hearing of their supplication, Knowing of their conditions.﴾

That is (a reference to) the good trial. Its position is nominative: meaning, the purpose is that, and that Allah weakens (mūhinu) the schemes of the disbelievers is coordinated with "that." He means: the purpose is to bestow trial (ibla') upon the believers and to weaken the scheme of the disbelievers. It is also read as mawhinu with the doubled letter (tashdid), and it is read with the genitive construction (idafa), and in its original form, which is tanwin and grammatical government (i'mal).

﴿If you seek victory, then victory has indeed come to you﴾. This is addressed to the people of Makkah in a mocking manner. When they wanted to set out, they clung to the curtains of the Ka'bah and said: "O God, grant victory to the one of us who is most generous to the guest, most connected to kin, and most effective in freeing captives. If Muhammad is upon the truth, then grant him victory, and if we are upon the truth, then grant us victory."

It is also narrated that they said: "O God, grant victory to the higher of the two armies, the more guided of the two groups, and the more honourable of the two parties."

It is narrated that Abu Jahl said on the day of Badr: "O God, whichever of us is more wrongful and more severing of kinship, destroy him today." That is, destroy him.

It was also said: "﴿If you seek victory﴾" is addressed to the believers, and "﴿and if you desist﴾" is addressed to the disbelievers. The meaning is: if you desist from hostility towards the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then ﴿it is better for you﴾ and safer; and ﴿if you return [to fighting him], We will return [to supporting him] against you﴾. "﴿And that God﴾" was read with a fatha, meaning: "and because God is the helper of the believers, that was so." It was also read with a kasra, and this is the more likely. The reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports it: "﴿and God is with the believers﴾." It was also read: "﴿and it will not avail you﴾" with a ya', for the separation of the verb from its subject.

And do not turn away from Him (﴿وَلَا تَوَلَّوْا عَنْهُ﴾). It has been read with one of the two tā's elided and assimilated (idghām) into the following letter, so that تَوَلَّوْا is read as تَوَلَّوْا with a single tā', as it is in the text. The pronoun in عَنْهُ refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because the meaning is: "And obey the Messenger of Allah," as in His saying: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [9:62]. Also, obedience to the Messenger and obedience to Allah are one thing, as in ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [4:80]. So the return of the pronoun to one of them is like its return to both of them, as when you say: "Kindness and generosity do not benefit so-and-so." It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the command to obey, meaning: "Do not turn away from this command and from carrying it out, while you are hearing it." Or it means: "Do not turn away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and do not oppose him." ﴿While you are hearing﴾, meaning you accept it as true, because you are believers, and you are not like the deaf deniers among the disbelievers. ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear,"﴾, meaning they claimed to hear, ﴿while they do not hear﴾, because they are not accepting it as true, so it is as if they were not hearing. The meaning is: you believe in the Qur'an and prophethood, so if you turn away from obeying the Messenger in some matters, such as the division of the spoils and other things, then your belief is no belief at all, and your hearing resembles the hearing of one who does not believe. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, the worst of the creatures (dawābb)﴾, meaning: indeed the worst of those that crawl upon the face of the earth. Or: indeed the worst of beasts are those who are deaf to the truth and do not understand it. He made them of the kind of beasts, then made them the worst of them. ﴿And if Allah had known any good (khayr) in these deaf and dumb ones﴾, meaning any benefit from His kindness (lutf), ﴿He would have made them hear﴾, by His kindness toward them, ﴿until they hear as those who accept the truth.﴾ Then He said: ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averse.﴾

[[Mahmud said: "That is, if Allah knew that kindness would benefit these people..." etc.]] Ahmad (ibn al-Munayyir) may Allah have mercy on him said: The unrestricted statement that Allah, exalted is He, shows kindness to the servant but His kindness does not benefit him is rejected. Kindness (lutf) is the bestowing of beauty and favor upon someone, and His name al-Latif derives from this. When He bestows a favor upon the servant by making him hear in a way that is kind to him, that is the desired goal. The meaning of kindness toward him on this view is that He creates in his heart the acceptance of the truth, good attentiveness to it, and guidance by it. But this does not hold according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (I'tizal) and the corrupt opinion about the creation of actions (khalq al-af'āl), because its implication is that the servant himself creates for himself the acceptance of the truth, guidance, good hearing and attentiveness, and that Allah, exalted is He, does not share with the servant in creating that. Rather, what is attributed to Allah, exalted is He, is the will for guidance from all creation, and it does not follow that His will is realized universally, exalted is Allah above what they say. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 24:

"When He calls you" — the pronoun is made singular here, as it was in the preceding verse, because the response to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the same as the response to Him, and the two are mentioned together only for emphasis. The meaning of "response" (istijabah) is obedience and compliance.

By "the call" (da'wah) is meant the rousing and urging. It is related on the authority of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by the door of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and called out to him while he was praying. He hastened through his prayer and then came and said: "What prevented you from answering me?" He said: "I was praying." He said: "Did you not find in what Allah revealed to me: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾?" He said: "Indeed, I will not, from now on, fail to answer you when you call me." [Related by al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i without the words "I will not... to the end"; Ibn Mardawayh related it by the same route as al-Tirmidhi, and at its end: "Indeed, I, O Messenger of Allah, will not fail to answer you when you call me, even if I am praying." In the same chapter there is a report from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, related by al-Bukhari with a different wording, and al-Tibi limited himself to it.]

On this there are two opinions. The first: this is something peculiar to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The second: his call was for a matter that could not bear delay, and when such a matter befalls one who is praying, he may break off his prayer.

"That which gives you life" refers to the sciences of religion and the laws, because knowledge is life, just as ignorance is death. And one of them said:

"Do not be impressed by the ignorant man and his finery, for he is a corpse, and his garment is a shroud." [Of al-Zamakhshari. It is a prohibition to the ignorant man against being vain and proud of his clothes, because he is like a corpse in being without benefit and without perception; it follows from this that the garment he admires is like a shroud, since it encloses a body with no perception and no benefit in it. Here "al-mayt" is with the light (takhfif) pronunciation.]

It is also said that it refers to fighting the disbelievers, for if they had abandoned it they would have overcome and killed them, like His saying: ﴿And in retribution there is life for you﴾. And it is said that it refers to martyrdom, based on His saying: ﴿Nay, they are alive with their Lord﴾.

"And know that Allah comes between a man and his heart" — meaning that He causes him to die, so the opportunity he has is lost to him. [Mahmud said: "its meaning is that He causes him to die, so the opportunity he possesses is lost to him..." etc. Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Yes, this is the creed of the People of the Sunnah, which the name "Mujbirah" was borrowed to describe; it is the true creed founded on piety and the entrusting of all creatures to the One True Creator of creation. If that is injustice, then I am innocent of the sect that calls itself "Adliyyah," persisting in this false opinion and this barren belief. And Allah is the Granter of success.] This opportunity is the ability to purify the heart, to treat its diseases and ailments, and to return it sound as Allah wills. So seize this opportunity, and purify your hearts for the obedience of Allah and His Messenger.

"And know that you will be gathered to Him" — so He will reward you according to the soundness of your hearts and the sincerity of your obedience.

It is also said: its meaning is that Allah may take possession of the servant's heart, dissolving his resolutions and changing his intentions and aims, replacing fear with security, security with fear, remembrance with forgetfulness, and forgetfulness with remembrance, and the like of that, which is permissible for Allah, exalted is He.

As for what the servant is rewarded or punished for among the actions of the heart, that is not so. [Al-Zamakhshari's words "as for what the servant is rewarded for... etc." — the question here is a branch of the question of the creation of humans' voluntary acts. According to the Mu'tazilah, the one who wills and creates them is the servant, and his obligation is valid because his choice is evident. According to the People of the Sunnah, the one who wills and creates them is Allah, exalted is He. The servant's obligation is valid because he has an acquisition (kasb) in them, which is a choice of some over others, as attested by immediate experience, in contrast to the Jabriyyah, who hold pure compulsion; its proper place is the discussion of tawhid.] The Jabriyyah hold that He comes between a man and faith if he disbelieves, and between him and disbelief if he believes — exalted is Allah far above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.

It is also said that its meaning is: He knows every thought that occurs to a man's mind, and nothing of his inner thoughts is hidden from Him, so it is as if He is between him and his heart.

It has been read as "bayna al-mar" with the letter ra' doubled. Its explanation is that the hamzah has been dropped and its vowel placed on the ra', as in "al-khabb," and then the pause was intended according to the dialect of those who say "marrtu bi-Umarr."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verses 25–26:

*Fitnah* (trial, affliction) means sin. It has been said that it is the tolerance of wrongdoing among them. It has also been said that it is the division of the word (of unity). And it has been said that *fitnah* means punishment.

As for His words ﴿لَا تُصِيبَنَّ﴾ (*"it will not strike"*), it can be one of three things: a response to a command, a prohibition following a command, or a description of *fitnah*. If it is a response, the meaning is: your affliction will not strike only the wrongdoers among you, but will encompass you all. This is like what is related about the scholars of the Children of Israel who forbade wrongdoing with a lax (*ta'dhir*) attitude, so God encompassed them all with punishment. [[His words "forbade wrongdoing with a lax attitude": *al-ta'dhir* in a matter means falling short in it. (al-Sihah). (ʿ)]]

If it is a prohibition following a command, it is as if it were said: "Beware of a sin or a punishment," and then it was said: "Do not expose yourselves to wrongdoing, lest the punishment or the consequence and harm of the sin strike those among you who did wrong, and not only them." Likewise, if you take it as a description, with the implied sense of speech, it is as if it were said: "And fear a trial about which it is said: ﴿it will not strike﴾."

Its parallel is the verse:

*Until, when the darkness grew thick and mingled,*
*They came with a mixture; have you ever seen the wolf?*

[[*Bitna bi-Hassan wa-ma'zahu yi'uttu,*
*yalhas udhnayhi wa-hinan yamtakhitu.*
*Ma ziltu as'a fihimu wa-akhtabitu,*
*hatta idha jannaʾl-zalamu wa-ikhtalatu,*
*jaʾu bi-madhqin hal ra'aytu al-dhi'ba qatu.*

Attributed to Ahmad al-Rajaz. It is also said to be by al-Ajjaj, describing a man as stingy. *Bata bi-l-qawm* means he arrived among the people at night. *Al-att* is the sound of the belly. *Al-ma'z* (with vowel variants) and *al-mu'ayyiz*, *al-am'uz* and *al-ma'za* are the opposite of sheep among goats; it is a collective noun, and the feminine *al-ma'za* is a dialectal form. *Al-ikhtibat* means seeking provision without guidance. The poet says: we alighted with Hassan at night, while his goats were hungry and emaciated. So *al-atit* is a metaphor for the first, and *al-amtakh* for the second. It is also possible that this is a metaphor for the large number of goats he had, and that he deceived them, offering them a mixture after a period in which he could have slaughtered a sheep for them. This is more fitting with what follows. The pronoun in *udhnayhi* may refer to the goats, since they are masculine according to most, or it may refer to Hassan, and this would be a severe insult. *Fihim* means "among them," i.e., among his tribe. *Jamma al-nabt* means it grew tall. *Al-layl* means it became dark. *Al-dhubab* means its sounds multiplied. *Al-zalam* means it became thick and mingled, its parts piled upon one another so that no light could pass through. *Al-madhq* is a mixture, meaning milk mixed with water. It is also transmitted as *bi-madhqin* with a kasra, which is that same milk. It is also transmitted as *bi-dayhin*, with a dotted letter, then a letter with two dots below, then an undotted letter, meaning the same as *madhq* but thinner. *Hal ra'ayta* is an interrogative of affirmation, and the clause is a description of *madhq*, i.e., a mixture about which this is said. The purpose is to liken the mixture to the wolf in its murkiness, and the interrogative is used to express this, because whoever wants to bring something to mind and picture it in imagination asks about it, as if he said: "Have you seen it?" and he replied "Yes." He then said: "The milk is like it," but all of this has been omitted and the interrogative suffices in its place. *Qatu* is an adverb built on a damma, with the pause marked by sukun.]]

That is, with a mixture about which this statement is said, because it is thin, with the color of the wolf's *waraqa* (dark tint). [[His words "because it is thin, with the color of the wolf's *waraqa*": *al-samar* is thin milk, and *tasmir al-laban* is thinning it with water. *Al-waraqa* is a whiteness inclining toward blackness and greenness. (al-Sihah). (ʿ)]]

The final meaning is reinforced by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿لَتُصِيبَنَّ﴾ (*"it will surely strike"*), as the answer to an omitted oath.

It is related from al-Hasan that this was revealed concerning ʿAli, ʿAmmar, Talha and al-Zubayr, specifically the Day of the Camel. al-Zubayr said: "It was revealed about us, and we recited it for a long time, and we did not think we were among its people, but then we became those it refers to." The meaning of khiyana (betrayal) is deficiency, just as the meaning of wafa' (fulfilment) is completeness. From it comes takhawwanahu, meaning he found a deficiency in him, and then it was used for the opposite of trustworthiness and fidelity, because when you betray a man in something you have introduced a deficiency into it. It has been used figuratively, so it is said: "the bucket's rope betrayed (khana) the well-rope," and "the honey-gatherer's cord betrayed (khana) the rope," because when it snaps under them it is as if it did not keep faith with them.

From this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿and do not betray your trusts﴾. The meaning is: do not betray God by neglecting His obligations, and do not betray His Messenger by not following his sunnah. "Your trusts" refers to what is between you, by not safeguarding them. ﴿while you know﴾ refers to the consequence and burden of that. It is also said: ﴿while you know﴾ means that you know you are betraying, meaning that the betrayal is found in you deliberately, not through forgetfulness. It is also said: ﴿while you are scholars who know the ugliness of the ugly and the goodness of the good﴾.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) refused except that they should submit to the judgement of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. They refused and said: "Send to us Abu Lubaba Marwan ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir," who was advising them, because his dependants and property were in their hands. So he was sent to them, and they said to him: "What do you think, should we submit to the judgement of Sa'd?" He pointed to his throat, meaning that it is slaughter. Abu Lubaba said: "My feet did not move until I knew that I had betrayed God and His Messenger. Then I came down." He tied himself to one of the pillars of the mosque and said: "By God, I will not taste food or drink until I die or God accepts my repentance." He remained for seven days until he fell unconscious. Then God accepted his repentance. It was said to him: "You have been forgiven, so release yourself." He said: "No, by God, I will not release myself until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is the one who releases me." So he came to him and untied him with his own hand. He said: "Part of the completeness of my repentance is that I should abandon the house of my people in which I committed the sin, and that I should strip myself of my wealth." It is also related from al-Mughira that it was revealed concerning the killing of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may God be pleased with him.

It is also said: ﴿your trusts﴾ means what God has entrusted you with of His obligations and limits.

So it is incumbent upon you to aspire to seek it (the great reward) and to what your resolves lead to, and to renounce the world, and not to be greedy for the accumulation of wealth and love of children, lest you ruin yourselves for their sake, as in His saying: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾, and the verse. It has also been said: this is among what was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah and his lapse because of his wealth and his children.

furqānan: victory (naṣran), because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and between disbelief through the humiliation of its party and Islam through the honouring of its people. From this is His saying, ﴿on the day of the criterion (yawm al-furqān)﴾. Or [it means] clarity and manifestation, making your affair known and spreading your renown and your traces throughout the regions of the earth, from their saying "I began (bittu) to do such-and-such," until the furqān shone forth, i.e., the dawn rose. Or [it means] a way out of doubts, success, and expansion of the breasts. Or [it means] a distinction between you and others among the people of other religions, and excellence and distinction in this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 30:

When God granted him victory, He mentioned the plot of the Quraysh against him while he was in Makkah, so that he would give thanks for God's blessing (ʿazza wa-jall) in delivering him from their scheming, in gaining mastery over them, and in the good outcome God granted him. The meaning is: remember when they plotted against you. This was because the Quraysh, when the Ansar had embraced Islam and pledged allegiance to him, feared that his affair would grow [[His saying "they feared that his affair would grow": i.e., they feared that his matter would become great. (Sihah, Lisan dictionary reference). (ʿ)]], so they gathered in Dar al-Nadwa (the council house of the Quraysh) to consult about his affair. Iblis entered upon them in the form of an old man and said: "I am an elder from Najd. I am not from Tihamah. I came to Makkah and heard of your gathering, so I wished to attend, and you will not lack from me opinion and sincere counsel." Abu al-Bakhtari said: "My opinion is that you imprison him in a room, bind his fetters, and seal its door except for a small opening through which you pass him his food and drink, and you wait for him to meet the fate of death." Iblis said: "Evil is this opinion. His people will come to fight you and rescue him from your hands." Hisham ibn ʿAmr said: "My opinion is that you mount him on a camel and expel him from among you; then he will not harm you by what he does, and you will be at rest." Iblis said: "Evil is this opinion. He will corrupt another people and fight you with them." Abu Jahl said: "I see that you should take from every clan a young man and give him a sharp sword, and they should strike him with the blow of a single man, so his blood is spread among the tribes. Then the Banu Hashim will not be able to fight all of the Quraysh, and if they ask for the blood-money, we will pay it and be at rest." The old man, may God curse him, said: "This young man has spoken truly; he is the best of you in opinion."

So they dispersed upon the opinion of Abu Jahl, united in killing him. Jibril (peace be upon him) informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and commanded him not to sleep in his bed, and God permitted him to emigrate. He commanded ʿAli (may God be pleased with him) to sleep in his bed, and said to him: "Wrap yourself in my cloak, for no harm you dislike will reach you." They spent the night watching, and when morning came they rushed to his bed, but they saw ʿAli and were confounded, and God (ʿazza wa-jall) frustrated their effort, and they followed his trail, but God nullified their scheme. [[The story was related by Ibn Ishaq in al-Maghazi: "Someone I do not accuse of lying related to me, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: 'When the Quraysh gathered in Dar al-Nadwa and consulted about the affair of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), Iblis confronted them in the form of an old man,' and he related it at length." Ibn Sa'd related it in the biography of Khalid ibn al-Walid through the route of al-Mughira ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, who said: Khalid ibn al-Walid said... and he mentioned the story of his conversion, and in it: 'Indeed Islam wipes out what was before it.' In the biography of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, from the narration of Ya'qub ibn Utba from al-Mughira, he mentioned the story of his conversion, and in it that. In the biography of Hibar ibn al-Aswad, from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im in the story of Hibar's conversion, and in it: 'And Islam wipes out what was before it.' In the chains of all three is al-Waqidi.]] They said: when a combatant (harbi) embraces Islam, no liability remains upon him at all; but as for a dhimmi, he is not obliged to make up the rights of Allah, while the rights of human beings remain upon him.

Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, argued by this that an apostate who embraces Islam is not obliged to make up the acts of worship he neglected during his apostasy and before it. He interpreted ﴿and if they return﴾ as apostasy. It was also read ﴿will be forgiven them﴾ with the pronoun referring to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Fight them until there is no more fitna (disbelief), meaning until no shirk at all remains among them, and religion is entirely for Allah, and every false religion vanishes from them, leaving the religion of Islam alone among them. But if they desist from disbelief and embrace Islam, then surely Allah is All-Seeing of what they do; He will reward them for their repentance and their Islam. It has also been read as ﴿تعملون﴾ with the ta', so the meaning becomes: surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do, of jihad in His way, calling to His religion, and bringing people out of the darkness of disbelief into the light of Islam; He will repay you with the best of rewards. But if they turn away and do not desist, then know that Allah is your Mawla (Protector), that is, your Helper and Supporter, so put your trust in His protection and His support.
