Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 41:

﴿Whatever you gain as booty﴾: "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah). "Min shay'" ("of anything") specifies it. It is said: "of anything," even a thread or a needle. "Fa-anna lillāhi" begins with "anna" as a subject whose predicate is omitted; its estimated form is: "then it is due," or "then it is obligatory, that God's is its fifth."

Al-Ju'fi narrated from Abu 'Amr: "fa-inna Allāhi" with a kasra. This is strengthened by the reading of al-Nakha'i: "fa-li-llāhi khumusahu." The well-known reading is more emphatic and more firmly establishes obligation, as if it were said: there must be an assurance of the fifth in it; there is no way to neglect it or be remiss about it. This is because when the predicate is omitted and more than one estimated predicate is possible, such as "fixed, obligatory, binding, necessary," and the like, it is stronger in obligation than stating one specific predicate. It is also read "khumusahu" with a sukun.

If you ask: What is the division of the khums (fifth)? I say: According to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ it was divided into five shares: one share for the Messenger of God ﷺ; one share for the near kin (dhawu l-qurba) from the Banu Hashim and the Banu l-Muttalib, excluding the Banu 'Abd Shams and the Banu Nawfal, who were entitled to it at that time through support and backing, based on what was narrated from 'Uthman and Jubayr ibn Mut'im, may God be pleased with them both, that they said to the Messenger of God ﷺ:

"These are your kinsmen, the Banu Hashim; we do not deny their merit, because of your position which God has made from them. Do you see our brothers, the Banu l-Muttalib? You gave them and withheld from us, though we and they are in one rank." He ﷺ said: "They have not separated from us in the Jahiliyya or in Islam. The Banu Hashim and the Banu l-Muttalib are one thing," and he interlaced his fingers [[Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah through the chain of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab from Jubayr ibn Mut'im in full, and it is in the Sahih except the phrase "they did not separate from us."]]. And three shares: for the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil). After the death of the Messenger of God ﷺ, his share lapses by his death, and likewise the share of the near kin; they are given only for their poverty, so they are equal to all other poor, and their wealthy are not given, so it is divided among the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer.

According to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, it is divided into five shares: a share for the Messenger of God ﷺ, which is spent on what he used to spend it on for the public interests of the Muslims, such as equipping the warriors with weapons and horses (al-kura') and the like. [[The phrase "from weapons and horses": al-kura' is a collective noun for horses (Sihah).]] And a share for the near kin, both their wealthy and their poor, divided among them, with the male receiving the equivalent of the portion of two females. The remainder goes to the three categories.

According to Malik ibn Anas, may God have mercy on him: the matter is entrusted to the judgment (ijtihad) of the imam; if he sees fit to divide it among these, he does so; if he sees fit to give some of them and not others, he does so; and if he sees others as more deserving and more important, then to others.

If you ask: What is the meaning of mentioning God, may He be exalted, and joining the Messenger and others with Him? I say: It may mean "for God and for the Messenger," meaning for the Messenger of God ﷺ, like His saying: ﴿God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾; and that by mentioning Him is intended the obligation of a sixth share, spent on one of the ways of drawing near (to God); and that by His saying ﴿so that God's is its fifth﴾ is intended that it is due that the khums be offered as a means of drawing near to Him and nothing else. Then He specified from the ways of drawing near these five, to favor them over others, like His saying: ﴿and Gabriel and Michael﴾. So according to the first possibility, it is the position of the two imams; and according to the second, what Abu al-'Aliya said:

That it is divided into six shares: a share for God, the Most High, spent on the door-ring (ratāj) of the Ka'ba [[In the Sihah, "al-ratj" with a fatha on the ta' is the great door, and likewise "al-ratāj"; and "tāj al-Ka'ba" (the crown of the Ka'ba).]]. And from him: The Messenger of God ﷺ would take the khums, strike his hand into it, take a handful from it, and place it for the Ka'ba, which is the share of God, the Most High; then he would divide what remained into five [[Narrated by Abu Dawud in Kitab al-Marasil through the chain of al-Rabi' ibn Anas from Abu al-'Aliya. He said: "When the Prophet ﷺ was brought spoils, he divided them into five parts, then he would grasp with his hand a handful from the whole khums and say: 'This is the Ka'ba.' Then he would say: 'Do not make for God a share, for to God belong the Hereafter and this world.' Then he would take one share for himself, one for the near kin, one for the orphans, one for the needy, and one for the wayfarer." Narrated by Abu 'Ubayd in al-Amwal and al-Tabari through this route.]]. It is also said: the share of God, the Most High, is for the public treasury (bayt al-mal). And according to the third, the position of Malik ibn Anas.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, that it was in six shares: for God and the Messenger, two shares; a share for his kin until he died. Then Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, made the khums into three. Likewise it is narrated from 'Umar and the caliphs after him.

It is narrated that Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, withheld the khums from the Banu Hashim and said: "What is due to you is that your poor be given, your unmarried be married, and those among you without a servant be served; as for your wealthy, they are like a wealthy wayfarer who is not given anything from charity, nor is a wealthy orphan."

From Zayd ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with him: he said the same: "It is not for us to build palaces from it, nor to ride thoroughbred mounts from it."

It is also said: the whole khums is for the kin.

From 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that it was said to him: "God, the Most High, said: ﴿and the orphans and the needy﴾," so he said: "Our orphans and our needy."

From al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him, concerning the share of the Messenger of God ﷺ: that it belongs to the ruler after him.

From al-Kalbi, may God be pleased with him, that the verse was revealed at Badr. Al-Waqidi said: the khums was in the expedition of Banu Qaynuqa', a month and three days after Badr, on the middle of Shawwal, at the head of twenty months from the Hijra.

If you ask: To what does His saying ﴿if you have believed in God﴾ relate? I say: It relates to an omitted element indicated by ﴿and know﴾. The meaning: if you have believed in God, then know that the khums of the booty must be offered as a means of drawing near (to God); so cut off your greed for it and be content with the four-fifths. The intended knowledge is not bare knowledge, but knowledge joined with action and obedience to God's command, because bare knowledge is shared by believer and disbeliever. ﴿And what We sent down﴾ is conjoined with "in God," meaning: if you have believed in God and in what We sent down ﴿upon Our servant﴾. It is also read "'abdinā" with two dammas, like His saying: ﴿and served the Taghut﴾. ﴿On the day of the Criterion﴾: the day of Badr. ﴿The two hosts﴾: the two groups of Muslims and disbelievers. The intended meaning is what was sent down to him of signs, angels, and victory on that day. ﴿And God is powerful over all things﴾: He is capable of granting victory to the few over the many, and the humble over the mighty, as He did for you that day.

﴿إِذْ﴾ is a substitute for "the Day of the Criterion" (yawm al-Furqan). *Al-'adwah* means the bank of a valley, and it may be read with a kasra, a damma or a fatha (*bi-l-kasr wa-l-ḍamm wa-l-fatḥ*). It has also been read as *bihinna* and as *al-'idwa*, with the waw changed to a ya', because there is a weak, non-solid barrier between it and the kasra, as in *al-ṣibyah*.

*Al-dunya* and *al-quṣwa* are the feminine forms of *al-adna* and *al-aqṣa*. If you ask: both are of the *fu'lā* pattern derived from a waw root, so why does one come with a ya' and the other with a waw? I answer: the analogical form is to change the waw into a ya', as in *al-'ulyā*. As for *al-quṣwā*, it comes in its original form, like *al-qawd*. *Al-quṣyā* has also been used, but the use of *al-quṣwā* is more common, just as *istaṣwaba* is more common than *istaṣāba*, and *aghīlat* is more common than *aghālat*. [[Qawluhu "wa-aghīlat ma'a aghālat": aghīlat means she nursed while she was pregnant (muwṭa'ah). Stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] *Al-'adwah al-dunya* is the side nearer to Madinah, and *al-quṣwā* is the side nearer to Makkah.

﴿وَالرَّكْبُ أَسْفَلَ مِنْكُمْ﴾: this means the forty riders who were leading the caravan, lower than you along the coast. *Asfal* is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning a place lower than your place, and its position is in the nominative, since it is the predicate of the subject.

If you ask: what is the benefit of this specification, and of mentioning the positions of the two groups and that the caravan was lower than them? I answer: the benefit is to inform about the condition that shows the strength of the enemy's position and power, the completeness of their numbers, and the smoothing of the means of victory for them. It also shows the weakness of the Muslims' situation and the confusion of their affairs [[Qawluhu "wa-l-iltiyāth amrihim": i.e., the confusion of their affairs (ikhtilāṭ amrihim), as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]], and that their victory in such a situation was nothing but a work of God, Glorified is He, and a proof that this was a matter that could not have been achieved except by His power, His strength and His overwhelming might. The side farther away, where the polytheists had camped, had water in it, and it was land that was not bad, whereas there was no water on the nearer side, and it was soft sand (*khabār*) [[Qawluhu "wa-hiya khabār": i.e., soft, with holes (ruKhwah dhāt juḥrah), as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] in which feet sink and in which one can walk only with fatigue and hardship. The caravan was behind the backs of the enemy, together with their great numbers, so the protection of it doubled their zeal and sharpened their resolve in fighting for it. For this reason the Arabs used to go out to war with their women and their wealth, so that the defence of the women and the protectiveness toward the sacred things would stir them to their utmost effort in fighting, and so that they would leave behind them nothing toward which they might incline their souls to retreat. This gathers their hearts, controls their resolve, and settles their souls on not leaving their positions or abandoning their stations, and on exerting the utmost of their support and their greatest firmness. In this there is also a depiction of what God, Glorified is He, had arranged concerning the event of Badr, in order to accomplish a matter that was decreed: the glorifying of His religion and the raising of His word. He had promised the Muslims one of the two groups, vaguely and without specification, so they went out intending to seize the caravan, unwilling to go out to fight. Quraysh set out in alarm at what had reached them of the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) targeting of their wealth, until they rushed out to protect their caravan. He arranged the causes until these people camped on the nearer side and those on the farther side, with the caravan behind them, and they defended it, until the war came to a head and what happened, happened.

﴿وَلَوْ تَوَاعَدْتُمْ﴾: even if you and the people of Makkah had made an appointment and agreed among yourselves on a time to meet for battle, some of you would have differed from others, and your small numbers and their large numbers would have hindered you from keeping the appointment, and what was in their hearts of awe of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the Muslims would have hindered them too. So there would not have come about for you a meeting like the one that God, may He be exalted, made possible and caused.

﴿لِيَقْضِيَ﴾ is connected to something omitted; that is, He arranged that to bring about a matter that had to be done, namely the victory of His allies and the subjugation of His enemies. His saying ﴿لِيَهْلِكَ﴾ is a substitute for it. Destruction and life are used metaphorically for disbelief and Islam, meaning: so that the disbelief of the one who disbelieved would proceed from clear evidence, not from the confusion of doubt, so that for him there would be no argument against God; and so that the Islam of the one who became Muslim would also proceed from certainty and knowledge that it is the religion of truth, which must be entered and held fast. This is because what happened at the battle of Badr was among the bright, luminous signs, and whoever disbelieved after them was being arrogant toward himself and deceiving himself.

It is also read *li-yahlika* with a fatha on the lam, and *ḥayya* with the doubling shown (*ibẓhār al-taḍ‘īf*).

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَسَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾: He knows how He manages your affairs and sets your interests in order. Or: He is Hearing and Knowing of the disbelief of the one who disbelieved and of his punishment, and of the belief of the one who believed and of his reward.

Surah 8, verse 43: "When Allah showed them to you in your dream as few. And if He had shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart and disputed about the matter, but Allah saved (you). Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf):

﴿إِذْ يُرِيكَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ is in the accusative (naṣb) by the implied verb "remember" (udhkur). Or it is a second substitute (badal thānī) for "the Day of the Criterion (yawm al-Furqān)", or it is connected to the words "indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing," meaning: He knows what is beneficial, when He made them seem few in your eyes ﴿فِي مَنامِكَ﴾ "in your dream." That is because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, showed them to him in his dream as few, and he informed his companions of that, so it was a reassurance to them and an encouragement against their enemy. And from al-Ḥasan: "in your dream" means "in your eye," because the eye is the place of sleep, just as the quilt (qaṭīfa) is called al-manāma, because one sleeps in it. [[His words "the quilt" refers to a velvet covering. (Ṣiḥāḥ). (ʿ)]]

This is an interpretation that contains strain (taʿassuf), and I do not think the report from al-Ḥasan is sound on it, nor does it suit his knowledge of the Arabic language and its eloquence. ﴿لَفَشِلْتُمْ﴾ "you would have lost heart," meaning you would have been cowardly and refrained from advancing, ﴿وَلَتَنازَعْتُمْ فِي الْأَمْرِ﴾ "and you would have disputed about the matter," and your word would have been divided in what you do, and you would have wavered between standing firm and fleeing. ﴿وَلكِنَّ اللَّهَ سَلَّمَ﴾ "but Allah saved," meaning He preserved and graciously granted safety from failure, dispute, and disagreement. ﴿إِنَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِذاتِ الصُّدُورِ﴾ "Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts," He knows what will come to be in them of boldness, cowardice, patience, and impatience.

And when He shows them to you as few in your eyes. The two pronouns are both objects: "when He lets you see them," meaning "when He causes you to see them." "Few" (qalilan) is accusative as a circumstantial (hal). He made them appear few in your eyes to confirm the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) vision, so that you would witness what he had told you, your certainty would increase, you would be resolute, and you would stand firm. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "They appeared so few in our eyes that I said to a man beside me, 'Do you think they are seventy?' He said, 'I think they are a hundred.' Then we captured one of them and asked him, 'How many were you?' He said, 'A thousand.'" [[Ishaq said in his Musnad: Amr ibn Muhammad and Yahya ibn Adam informed us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Ubaydah, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and he mentioned it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted it by this route.]] "And He makes you appear few in their eyes," until one of them said, "They are only a handful who would feast on a slaughtered camel." If you ask: the purpose of making the disbelievers appear few in the eyes of the believers is clear, so what is the purpose of making the believers appear few in the eyes of the disbelievers? I say: He made them appear few in their eyes before the encounter, then made them appear numerous in their eyes after it, so that they would be emboldened against them out of disregard for them; then the abundance would suddenly overtake them, so that they would be stunned and awed, and their strength would be broken ("wa-tafulla shawkatuhum," meaning it would be shattered, as stated in al-Sihah) when they see what was not in their calculation and estimation. This is His saying: "They see them as twice their number with their own eyes," and so that they would not prepare themselves against them, and so that the proof against them would be more evident through the clear sign, from their fewness at first and their multitude at the end. If you ask: by what means do they see the many as few? I say: Allah conceals part of them with a veil, or He alters something in their eyes so that they perceive the many as few, just as He altered the eyes of the squint-eyed so that they see one as two. It was said to one of them: "The squint-eyed sees one as two," and there was one rooster before him, so he said:

"Why do I not see these two roosters as four?"

﴿إِذا لَقِيتُمْ فِئَةً﴾ ("When you meet a company [of the enemy]"): that is, when you fight a group of the disbelievers. He omitted describing them because the believers only met disbelievers. Al-liqa' (encounter) is commonly used as a term for fighting.

﴿فَاثْبُتُوا﴾ ("then stand firm") for fighting them, and do not flee.

﴿وَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ كَثِيراً﴾ ("and remember Allah much"): in the places of war, seeking support through His remembrance, seeking victory through Him, and calling upon Him against your enemy: "O Allah, forsake them! O Allah, cut off their root!"

﴿لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ﴾ ("so that you may prosper"): so that you may attain your aims of victory and reward.

In this there is an indication that the servant should not slacken in the remembrance of his Lord, even when his heart is most preoccupied and most anxious, and that his soul should remain gathered for that remembrance even when it is scattered by other things. Enough as evidence of this is what is found in the sermons of Amir al-Mu'minin (the Commander of the Faithful), peace be upon him, during the days of Siffin and in his battles with the rebels (al-bughat) and the Khawarij (the Kharijites), of eloquence, clarity, subtle meanings, and eloquent admonitions and advice. (They show) that nothing distracted them from the remembrance of Allah, even when matters grew severe.

﴿وَلا تَنازَعُوا﴾ ("and do not dispute"): it is read with the letter ta' doubled. ﴿فَتَفْشَلُوا﴾ ("lest you lose heart") is in the subjunctive by the implied "an," or in the jussive because it falls under the sense of the prohibition. The reading of the one who read ﴿وَتَذْهَبَ رِيحُكُمْ﴾ ("and your strength depart") with ta' and the subjunctive, and the reading of the one who read "wa-yadhhab rikhukum" with ya' and the jussive, both indicate these two possibilities.

Al-rih (lit. "wind") means dominion (al-dawla): it was likened to the wind in the penetration and sweep of its command, and in its blowing. So it is said: "The winds of so-and-so blew," when dominion came to him and his command took effect. From this is his saying:

*O my two companions, is there none in the valley*
*except Ubayd, sitting among the camel-herds?*

*Will you wait a little for the moment of their heedlessness,*
*or will you run? For the wind belongs to the one who hastens.*

[[This verse is by Sulayk ibn Sulaka. He passed with his two companions through the bottom of a valley in Yemen called Murad, and they found camels that filled it. He said to them: "Wait for me here until I go to the herdsmen and learn the news of the tribe, whether they are near or far." He kept coaxing them until they told him the location of the tribe, and they were far away. He said to them: "Shall I not make you rich?" They said: "Yes." So he sang the two verses at the top of his voice, and his two companions came to him and drove off the camels.

"Amm" (with a long vowel) is in the plural. It is said: it is the plural of *imma'* (the plural of *amah*, "female slave"). It is also said: it is itself the plural of *amah*, so its origin is *a'muw*, like *adhru'* (the plural of *dhira'*). On the second view it is also *a'muw*, like *a'kum* (the plural of *akmah*), because the origin of *amah* is *amawah*. The second hamza was changed to an alif in the plural, the waw was changed to a ya' because it came at the end, and the hamza was given a kasra for harmony with it, then it was subjected to the same kind of irregular change as *qadin*. In another version, "qu'ud" is used instead of it. "Dhawd" (of camels) means from three to ten. "Atnzaranni" (lit. "will you wait for me") comes from *anzartuhu*, "I delayed him." "Rayth" means delay and lingering, and it is in the accusative as a substitute for "qalilan" (a little), or as an adverb of time. It is permissible to read "Atanzaran" from *nazarahu*, "I waited for him," so *rayth* may be its direct object. "Wa-ta'dwan" comes from *al-'adw*, meaning quick travel, or from *al-'udwan*, meaning transgressing the limit. He used "wind" metaphorically for dominion and an effective command, by the common element of penetration. It is also transmitted as "taghdwan" and "lil-ghadi" with a ghayn, meaning: "Will you hasten toward it? For victory belongs to the one who hastens." In this there is evidence that haste is better than delay.]]

It was also said: victory never came except by a wind that Allah, exalted is He, sends. In a hadith: "I was helped by the *saba'* (east wind), and 'Ad was destroyed by the *dabur* (west wind)."

[[Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh, i.e., reported by al-Bukhari and Muslim), through the chain of Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas.]]

﴿فَاثْبُتُوا﴾ ("then stand firm") for fighting them, and do not flee.

﴿وَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ كَثِيراً﴾ ("and remember Allah much"): in the places of war, seeking support through His remembrance, seeking victory through Him, and calling upon Him against your enemy: "O Allah, forsake them! O Allah, cut off their root!"

﴿وَلا تَنازَعُوا﴾ ("and do not dispute"): it is read with the letter ta' doubled. ﴿فَتَفْشَلُوا﴾ ("lest you lose heart") is in the subjunctive by the implied "an," or in the jussive because it falls under the sense of the prohibition. Al-rih (lit. "wind") means dominion (al-dawla): it was likened to the wind in the penetration and sweep of its command, and in its blowing. So it is said: "The winds of so-and-so blew," when dominion came to him and his command took effect. From this is his saying:

*O my two companions, is there none in the valley*
*except Ubayd, sitting among the camel-herds?*

*Will you wait a little for the moment of their heedlessness,*
*or will you run? For the wind belongs to the one who hastens.*

Warn them, by forbidding dispute and divergence of opinion, against the like of what befell those at Uhud for their opposition to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): their faintheartedness and the departure of their strength. Like those who went forth from their homes: these are the people of Makkah, who set out to protect the caravan. Abu Sufyan's messenger came to them while they were at al-Juhfah, saying: "Turn back, for your caravan has been saved." But Abu Jahl refused and said: "We will not turn back until we reach Badr, where we will drink wine, have singing-girls play music for us, and feed those Arabs who are with us." They went on and met it, and they were given the cups of death instead of wine, and mourning women wailed over them instead of singing-girls. So He forbade them to be like them, insolent and vain, showing off with their deeds, and commanded them to be among the people of piety, sorrow and grief from fear of God, the Mighty and Majestic, sincerely dedicating their deeds to God.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 48:

Remember when ﴿Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾, the deeds they had done in opposing the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He whispered to them that they could not be defeated and could not be overcome, and he gave them the illusion that following the footsteps (khutuwat) of Satan and obeying him would protect them. ﴿So when the two hosts met, he turned back on his heels and said, "I am free of you."﴾ That is, his scheming came to nothing when the hosts of God descended. Likewise, on the authority of al-Hasan (may God have mercy on him): this happened by way of whispering, and he did not appear to them in any form.

It was also said: when Quraysh gathered to set out, they recalled the war that lay between them and the Banu Kinanah, and this held them back. So Iblis appeared to them in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum, the Kinanite poet, who was one of their nobles, along with a host of devils, and he had a banner. He said, "No one can overcome you today, and I am your protector against the Banu Kinanah." When he saw the angels descending, he turned back. It was also said: his hand was in the hand of al-Harith ibn Hisham. When he turned back, al-Harith said to him, "Where are you going? Will you abandon us in this situation?" He said, "I see what you do not see," and he pushed al-Harith in the chest and departed. They were routed, and when they reached Makkah they said, "Suraqah has defeated the people." When news of this reached Suraqah, he said, "By God, I did not know of your departure until your defeat reached me." When they became Muslims, they realised that it had been Satan.

In a hadith: "Iblis was never seen on any day more humiliated (asghar), more repelled (adhar), or more enraged than on the Day of 'Arafah, because of what he sees of the descent of mercy; except what was seen on the Day of Badr."¹

(Footnote) ¹ "Wa la adhar": al-dahur means expulsion and removal from one's place (from al-Sihah of al-Jawhari). (ʿ)

(Footnote) ² Malik narrated it in al-Muwatta' from the transmission of Talhah ibn 'Ubaydullah ibn Kurayz as a mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain). Through Malik's route it was also transmitted by 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tabari, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman. Abu al-Nadr Isma'il ibn Ibrahim al-'Ijli alone differed from Malik by saying: "from Talhah, from his father." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: the correct version is the mursal. Note: this Talhah is Talhah ibn 'Abdullah ibn Bukayr, and Kurayz is a diminutive. In al-Manasik of al-Nawawi, it occurs as Talhah ibn 'Abdullah, one of the Ten (promised Paradise), and this is a clear error.

If you say: why was it not said, "La ghaliban lakum" (no overcomer for you), as one would say, "La darriban Zaydan 'indana" (no one is striking Zayd here)? I reply: if lakum were the object of ghalib, meaning "not overcoming you," then your statement would be correct. But it is a predicate, its implied sense being: "No overcomer exists for you."

When the hypocrites in Medina and those in whose hearts is a disease say, "These have been deceived by their religion." The phrase "those in whose hearts is a disease" may be an attribute of the hypocrites, or it may mean those who are on the edge, who are not firm-footed in Islam. It is also reported from al-Hasan that they are the polytheists. "These have been deceived by their religion": they mean that the Muslims were deluded by their religion, that they believed it would strengthen them and grant them victory for its sake, so they went out, though they were three hundred and some odd ten, against about a thousand. Then He said, in reply to them: ﴿And whoever puts his trust in Allah, then indeed Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾, that is, Mighty and Victorious, who empowers the few and weak over the many and strong.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verses 50–51:**

﴿Had you but seen﴾ (*wa-law tara*): had you witnessed and observed it. The particle «لو» (*law*, "if") turns the present tense into the meaning of the past, just as «إن» (*in*, "if") turns the past into the meaning of the future.

﴿When﴾ (*idh*) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*, an adverbial expression of time or place). It is also read as «يتوفى» (*yatawaffa*, "takes [them] in death") with the verb in the masculine (ي) and in the feminine (ت) forms.

﴿The angels﴾ (*al-malā'ikah*) is in the nominative because it is the subject of the verb. ﴿Striking﴾ (*yaḍribūna*) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to them. It is also permissible for the pronoun in «يتوفى» to refer to God, may He be exalted, with «الملائكة» in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, and «يضربون» as its predicate.

It is related from Mujahid: ﴿and their backs﴾ (*wa-adbārahum*) means their buttocks (*astāhum*). But God is generous and uses euphemism. They specifically mentioned these because the disgrace and the punishment are at their most severe when striking them. I have been told that the people of China have the following punishment for the adulterer: he is made to wait, then a strong man is given an iron implement shaped like a tray, heavy in weight and with a handle. He strikes the adulterer's rear with it in one powerful blow, and the man freezes in his place.

It was also said: they strike whatever is in front of them and whatever is behind them.

﴿And taste⟩ (*wa-dhūqū*) is coordinated with «يضربون» (*yaḍribūna*), taking the sense of "saying": that is, "and they say: taste." ﴿The punishment of the burning﴾ (*ʿadhāba al-ḥarīq*), that is, the first installment of the punishment of the Fire. Or ﴿taste the punishment of the Hereafter⟩, as good news to them of it. It was also said: they had iron maces with them, and whenever they struck with them the fire flared up. Or it is said to them on the Day of Resurrection: "Taste."

The answer to «لو» (*law*) is omitted; that is: you would have seen a dreadful and abhorrent matter.

﴿That﴾ (*dhālika*) is for what your hands have sent forth. It may be from God's speech and from the speech of the angels. ﴿That﴾ (*dhālika*) is the subject of a nominal sentence, and ﴿for what your hands have sent forth﴾ (*bimā qaddamat aydīkum*) is its predicate. ﴿And that God⟩ (*wa-anna Allāha*) is coordinated with it. That is: that punishment is due to two causes: because of your disbelief and your sins, and because ﴿God is not unjust to the servants⟩ (*laysa bi-ẓallāmin lil-ʿabīd*), since punishing the disbelievers is part of justice, just as rewarding the believers is.

It was also said: «ظلام» (*ẓallām*, "unjust") here is in the intensive form, "for the sake of the servants," meaning that He is not unjust to them in a great degree.

[Mahmud said: "It was also said: «ظلام» is for intensification, for the sake of the servants..." Ahmad said: With this point one answers the objection of the speaker who says: negating the lesser is more eloquent than negating the greater, so why was the more eloquent form abandoned? The purpose is to declare God exalted above injustice, and He is worthy of emphasis. So these two answers are ready at hand for this question.]

Or, because the punishment is so great that, were it not deserved, the one punished with its like would be an extreme oppressor, of intensely grave injustice.

The kāf in محل الرفع (in the nominative position): meaning, the custom (دأب) of these people is like the custom of the family of Pharaoh. Their daʾb (دأبهم) is their habit and practice, the thing they persisted in: that is, they continued at it and were constant in it. And "they disbelieved" (وَكَفَرُوا) is an explanation of the daʾb of the family of Pharaoh. And "that" (وذلِكَ) refers to what befell them, meaning that punishment or retribution, because of the fact that God, in His wisdom, does not and it is not fitting for Him to change a blessing He has given to a people until they change what is within themselves (حَتَّى يُغَيِّرُوا ما بهم من الحال). If you say: what change did the family of Pharaoh and the idolaters of Mecca make, such that God changed His blessing upon them? For they had no pleasing state that they might alter into a displeasing one. I say: just as a pleasing state changes into a displeasing one, a displeasing state changes into one more displeasing than it. Those people, before the Messenger was sent to them, were disbelievers and idol-worshippers. Then when he was sent to them with the clear signs, they denied him, opposed him, formed factions against him, and strove to shed his blood, so they changed their state to one worse than it had been. Thus God changed the respite He had granted them and hastened punishment upon them. And (وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ) God is All-Hearing of what those who deny the messengers say, (عَلِيمٌ) All-Knowing of what they do. (كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ) "Like the custom of the family of Pharaoh" is a repetition for emphasis. And in His saying (بِآياتِ رَبِّهِمْ) "with the signs of their Lord" there is further indication of the ingratitude for blessings and the denial of the truth. And in the mention of drowning (الإغراق) there is an explanation of the seizing for sins. (وَكُلٌّ كانُوا ظالِمِينَ) "And all of them were wrongdoers": all of them, both the drowned Copts and the slain of Quraysh, were wrongdoers to themselves through disbelief and disobedience.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 58:

﴿And if you fear treachery from a people with whom you have a treaty, then throw back to them [their covenant] on equal terms.﴾ That is, cast the covenant back at them, openly and on a straight, level course. This means that you should make known to them the cancellation of the treaty between you and them, and inform them plainly and clearly that you have severed what was between you and them. You should not attack them while they still suppose the covenant to be in force, for that would be treachery on your part. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous.﴾ So let there be no concealment on your part of the breaking of the covenant, and no deception.

It has also been said: "on equal terms in knowledge of the annulment of the covenant." And it has been said: "on equal terms in enmity."

The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur, "the prepositional phrase") is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal), as if it were said: "Throw back to them, standing firm upon a course of straightforward intent," or "while you and they are on equal terms in knowledge or in enmity." It is a circumstantial qualifier relating both to the one who throws back (al-nabidh) and to those to whom it is thrown back (al-manbudh ilayhim) together.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 59:

"سَبَقُوا" means they escaped and got away from being overtaken. "إِنَّهُمْ لا يُعْجِزُونَ" means: ﴿indeed they cannot escape﴾; they will not get away, and their pursuer will not find himself unable to overtake them.

It is recited also as "أنهم" with a fatha, meaning "لأنهم" (because they). Each of the kasra and fatha readings is a causal explanation, except that the kasra reading is in the manner of a resumed statement (isti'naf), while the fatha reading is an explicit causal explanation.

It is also recited "يعجزون" with tashdid (intensification of the ‘ayn). Ibn Muhaysin recited "يعجزون" with a kasra on the nun. Al-A'mash recited "ولا تحسب الذين كفروا" with a kasra and with a fatha on the ba', on the elision of the light nun (al-nun al-khafifa). Hamza recited "ولا يحسبن" with the ya' (the verb being attributed to those who disbelieved). It has been said about it: the original was "أن سبقوا", so the "أن" was elided, like His saying ﴿وَمِنْ آياتِهِ يُرِيكُمُ الْبَرْقَ﴾ [And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning]; and it is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "أنهم سبقوا". It has also been said: the verb governs "أنهم لا يعجزون", with "لا" being superfluous (silah), and "سبقوا" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "sabiqin", i.e. escaping and fleeing. It has also been said that its meaning is: ﴿and let not those who disbelieved think them to have escaped﴾, the pronoun being omitted because it is understood. And it has been said: "ولا يحسبن قبيل المؤمنين الذين كفروا سبقوا" (the group of believers should not think that those who disbelieved have escaped). All these opinions are strained, and this reading which Hamza uniquely adopted is not without precedent. It is related from al-Zuhri that it was revealed concerning those who escaped from the remnant of the polytheists.

from ﴿strength﴾: from everything by which one gains strength in war, in its various kinds. It is narrated from ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say on the pulpit: 'Indeed, strength is archery [[Narrated by Muslim, in a fuller version.]]'" He said it three times. ʿUqba died leaving seventy bows in the way of Allah.

[[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "The strength is archery; it was narrated by ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir that it is archery... etc." Ahmad said: "What corresponds to archery is that al-ribat (garrisoning) be on its original basis as a verbal noun, and Allah knows best. He is sufficient for me, and the best Disposer of affairs."]]

It is narrated from ʿIkrimah: it means fortresses. And ribat (the tethering or garrisoning of horses) is a name for the horses that are tethered in the way of Allah. It is permissible to call them ribat, which carries the meaning of murabatah (standing guard on the frontier). It is also permissible that it is the plural of rabit, like faṣīl and faṣāl. Al-Hasan recited "wa-min rubṭ al-khayl" with a dammah and with a sukun on the bāʾ, as the plural of ribāṭ.

It is also permissible that His words ﴿and from the horses held ready﴾ are a specification of horses from among what one gains strength with, like His words ﴿and Gabriel and Michael﴾.

It is narrated from Ibn Sirin, may Allah have mercy on him, that he was asked about someone who bequeathed a third of his wealth for fortresses. He said: "It is to be spent on horses, which are tethered and ridden in the way of Allah." It was said to him: "He only bequeathed it for fortresses." He said: "Have you not heard the words of the poet:

Verily the fortresses are horses, not the mud-built villages.
[[And indeed I have known, despite my avoiding destruction... that the fortresses are horses. The poet al-Ashʿar al-Jaʿfi said, meaning: I have become certain, though I avoid destruction, that the fortresses which protect from it are horses and the instruments of war, not buildings like the castles in villages. He said "despite my avoiding destruction" to ward off the assumption that he is a man who throws himself into ruin, and therefore loves war; it is thus an instance of ihtiras (precaution against misunderstanding). It is also narrated as "ʿalā tawaqqī al-radā" with the yāʾ doubled, meaning: while I am guarding against ruin."]]

A man said to ʿUbayd Allah ibn al-Hasan: "My father bequeathed a third of his wealth for fortresses." He said: "Go and buy horses with it." He said: "He only mentioned fortresses." So he said: "Have you not heard the verse of al-Ashʿar?" and he recited the verse.

﴿you terrify﴾: it is read with tashdīd and with takhfīf. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "tukhzūna". The pronoun in ﴿with it﴾ refers to ﴿what you can muster﴾.

﴿the enemy of Allah and your enemy﴾: they are the people of Makkah.

﴿and others besides them﴾: they are the Jews. It was also said: the hypocrites. It is narrated from al-Suddi that they are the people of Persia. It was said: the disbelieving jinn. There is a report in a ḥadīth: "Indeed, Satan does not approach the owner of a horse or a house in which there is a noble horse." It is also narrated that the neighing of horses terrifies the jinn.

[[I did not find it in this form. Ibn Saʿd, al-Tabarani and Ibn ʿAdi narrated it through the route of Saʿid ibn Sinan from Yazid ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUrayb from his father from his grandfather, raised to the Prophet regarding His words ﴿and others besides them﴾, the verse; he said: "They are the jinn, and Satan will not seize a person in whose house is a noble horse." Its isnad includes Ibn ʿAdi and Saʿid ibn Sinan, whom Ibn Maʿin and others declared weak. It has a supporting report from al-Waḍin ibn ʿAṭāʾ from Sulayman ibn Musa, as a mursal (a report whose chain omits the Companion). Ibn Mardawayh narrated through al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding this verse: "It is Satan; he does not approach the forelock of a horse," and its isnad is weak (wāh). As for his words "It is narrated that the neighing of horses drives away the jinn," I did not find it.]]

Janaha lahu wa-ilayhi: idha mala (he inclined to him, or toward it, when he leaned toward it). Al-silm (peace) is feminine, treated as the feminine form of its opposite, which is war (al-harb). The poet says:

"Take from it (peace) what you are content with, and war will suffice you with a few sips of its breaths."

[[Its explanation is given in the first volume, page 252, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector's note.]]

It is also read with the sin vowelled with fatha and with kasra (al-salm and al-silm). It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the verse is abrogated by the words of the Exalted: "Fight those who do not believe in Allah" (Qur'an 9:29). It is reported from Mujahid that it is abrogated by His words: "Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them" (Qur'an 9:5).

The sound view is that the command depends on what the Imam sees as beneficial for Islam and its people, whether war or peace. It is not binding that they must always be fought, nor that they must always be answered with a truce.

Al-Ashhab al-Uqayli read "fa-ujnah" with a damma on the nun. "And rely upon Allah" (Qur'an 8:61), and do not fear their concealed deceit in their inclination toward peace, for Allah is sufficient for you and will protect you from their plotting and treachery. Mujahid said: he means Qurayza.

فَإِنَّ حَسْبَكَ اللَّهُ ﴿Indeed, Allah is sufficient for you﴾. قال جرير:

إنِّى وَجَدْتُ مِنَ الْمَكارِمِ حَسْبَكُمْ ... أَنْ تَلْبَسُوا خَزَّ الثِّيَابِ وَتَشْبَعُوا [[إنى وجدت من المكارم حسبكم ... أن تلبسوا خز الثياب وتشبعوا

فإذا تذوكرت المكارم مرة ... في مجلس أنتم به فتقنعوا

لجرير، أى: إنى وجدت كافيكم من المكارم ليس الخز من الثياب والشبع من الطعام والشراب، وجعلهما من المكارم تهكما بهم. أو على زعمهم، أو المعنى: مغنيكم عنها هاتان الخصلتان، فمن للبدل، أو المعنى: إن كان ذلك من المكارم فهو كافيكم لمبالغتكم فيه. ويروى: حر الثياب، بمهملتين، أى جيدها. وتذوكرت: مبنى للمجهول، أى: فإذا تذاكر الناس بالمكارم ولو مرة واحدة فغطوا وجوهكم حياء كالنساء فلستم من المكارم في شيء.]]

(Jarir said:)

"I have found that of nobility, your sufficiency is this: that you wear the silk of garments and fill your bellies.
So when nobility is mentioned once in an assembly where you are present, you veil yourselves."

Jarir's meaning: I have found that what suffices you of nobility is not silk garments, nor filling yourselves with food and drink, and he counted these as nobility in mockery of them, or according to their own claim. Or the meaning is: these two qualities suffice you in place of it, so the particle *min* (من) is for substitution (*lil-badal*). Or the meaning is: if that counts as nobility, then it suffices you because of your excessive pursuit of it. It is also narrated as *ḥarr al-thiyāb* (حر الثياب) with two unmarked letters, meaning its finest part. *Tudhukkirat* (تذوكرت) is in the passive voice, meaning: when people mention nobility, even once, you cover your faces out of shame like women, and you have no share of nobility at all.

وَأَلَّفَ بَيْنَ قُلُوبِهِمْ ﴿and He joined their hearts together﴾. The joining together of the hearts of those to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent is among the remarkable signs, because the Arabs, on account of the *ḥamiyya* (fierce protectiveness) and *'aṣabiyya* (tribal partisanship) within them, and their holding of rancour over the smallest matter and throwing it before their eyes until they take revenge, hardly any two of their hearts could be brought into agreement. Then their hearts came together in following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they became united, and they began to shoot from one bow. That was because of the bond of affection that Allah arranged among them, the unity of their word that He gathered, the love and mutual friendship that He produced between them, the hatred and enmity He removed from them, and the love for the sake of Allah and hatred for the sake of Allah that He imposed upon them. None can do this except One who possesses the hearts; He turns them as He wills and does in them what He intends.

It is said: they are the Aws and the Khazraj. Between them there were wars and battles that destroyed their chieftains and leaders and crushed their skulls, and their enmities had no limit or end. Between them was also the proximity of dwelling, which stirs up rancour and perpetuates envy and rivalry. It is the custom of any two groups in such a situation that each shuns what the other prefers and hates it and turns away from it. Yet Allah, exalted is He, made them forget all of that, until they agreed upon obedience, became sincere toward one another, became helpers, and became allies. This was nothing but by His subtle workmanship and His far-reaching power.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 64:

وَمَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ: The waw here carries the meaning of "with" (ma'iyya), and what follows it is in the accusative. You say: ḥasbuka wa-Zaydan dirham (enough for you and Zayd is a dirham). It is not put in the genitive, because coordinating an apparent noun in the genitive onto a pronominal suffix is impermissible. He says:

فَحَسْبُكَ وَالضَّحَّاكَ عَضْبٌ مُهَنَّدُ [[إذا كانت الهيجاء واشتقت العصا ... فحسبك والضحاك سيف مهتد

He means: when war breaks out, the staff splits (ashtaqqat al-'aṣā), meaning the community is divided, disagreement arises and evil appears, then a sword of Indian steel, polished and keen, is sufficient for you along with al-Ḍaḥḥāk. The splitting of the staff is a metaphor for the occurrence of discord and the appearance of evil. Ḥasb is a verb-like noun (ism fi'l) meaning "is sufficient," and the kaf is its object.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk is the object "with" (maf'ūl ma'ahu). Sayf is its subject. The majority hold that it is a descriptive adjective (ṣifa mushabbaha) in the sense of "sufficient," functioning as the subject (mubtada'), with the kaf as the attached pronoun (muḍāf ilayhi).

Sayf is its predicate (khabar). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk is the object of an implied verb, meaning "suffices," because the descriptive adjective does not govern an object "with." The reading al-Ḍaḥḥāk in the genitive is also reported, meaning "and [sufficient is] al-Ḍaḥḥāk," and in the nominative by taking the place of the omitted ḥasb. The waw is "with" according to the first reading, and coordinating according to other readings. It is also reported as: ʿaḍb muhannad. The ʿaḍb is the cutting sword.

The meaning: Allah is sufficient for you and for those believers who follow you as a helper. Or it may be in the nominative position: meaning Allah suffices you and the believers suffice you. This verse was revealed at al-Bayḍāʾ during the Battle of Badr before the fighting. And from Ibn ʿAbbas (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) it is reported that it was revealed concerning the conversion of ʿUmar (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu). And from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, that thirty-three men and six women had embraced Islam with the Prophet (ﷺ), then ʿUmar embraced Islam, and it was then revealed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verses 65–66:

Al-tahrid (incitement): intensifying the urging to a matter, derived from al-harad (ḥarḍ), which is when illness wears a person down and is so extreme that he approaches death; or it means that you call him "ḥarḍ," saying to him: "I see you only as one worn down (ḥarḍ) in this matter and made ill (mumrad) by it," in order to stir him up and move him. It is said: harrakahu, ḥarraḍahu, ḥarṣahu, ḥarashahu and ḥarrabahu, all with the same meaning. It is also read as ḥarras, with the unpointed ṣād, related by al-Akhfash, from al-ḥirṣ (eagerness). This is a promise from God and a good tidings that if a group of believers is patient, they will overcome ten times their number of unbelievers, by God's help and support. Then He said: ﴿bi-annahum qawmun la yafqahun﴾ (because they are a people who do not understand), meaning: because the unbelievers are an ignorant people who fight without seeking reward or hoping for recompense, like cattle; so their steadfastness is small, and they are deprived of God's victory because of their ignorance of Him, and they deserve His abandonment. This is unlike one who fights with insight and possesses what merits victory and manifestation from God, the Exalted.

It is related from Ibn Jurayj: "It was incumbent upon them not to flee, and each one of them was to stand firm against ten." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had sent Hamzah (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) with thirty riders, and he met Abu Jahl with three hundred riders. It is said: then this became burdensome for them and they complained of it, and that was after a long time, so it was abrogated (nusikha) and lightened for them, so that one could stand against two. It is also said: at the beginning they were few, and then when they increased, the lightening was revealed.

It is read ḍuʿafan with a fatḥah and with a ḍammah, like al-makth and al-mukth, and al-faqr and al-fuqr. Ḍuʿafa is the plural of ḍaʿif (weak). The verb attributed to "one hundred" is read with the feminine ta and with the masculine ya in both places. The meaning of ḍaʿf is weakness of body. It is also said: weakness of insight and of steadfastness in religion, and they varied in this.

He consulted Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) about them.[[Muslim narrated it from Ibn Abbas from Umar in a long hadith, and part of it has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah. They said: Yes, we will take the ransom, and they will be martyred" was narrated by al-Tabari through Ash'ath ibn Sawwar from Muhammad ibn Sirin from Ubayda, that is Ibn Amr, who said: "The Muslims took seventy captives from the polytheists and killed seventy. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set for them forty ounces of gold each, and set for his uncle al-Abbas one hundred ounces, and for Aqil eighty." The relatives said: "You have done this..." [the hadith continues].]]

It is also narrated that when they took the ransom, the verse was revealed. Umar entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and behold, he and Abu Bakr were weeping. Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me. If I find [a reason for] weeping I will weep, and if I do not find it, I will feign weeping." He said: "I weep over your companions for their taking of the ransom. It is also narrated that he said: "Had a punishment descended from the sky, none would have been saved from it except Umar and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with both of them, because of his saying: 'Subduing in killing is more beloved to me.'"[[Al-Tabari narrated through Ibn Ishaq, who said: "None of the believers who were present at Badr loved the spoils except Umar ibn al-Khattab, for he would not meet a captive without striking his neck. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Had a punishment descended from the sky, none would have been saved from it except Umar ibn al-Khattab and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.'" Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet: "Had the punishment come down, none would have escaped it except Ibn al-Khattab."]]

﴿ʿarḍa al-dunyā﴾ means "the goods of this world," its passing possessions. It was so named because it is a transient thing that stays only briefly; he means the ransom. ﴿Allah desires the Hereafter﴾, that is, what causes Paradise, namely the exaltation of Islam through subduing in killing.

It is also recited as ﴿yurīdūna﴾ ("they desire") with the letter *yā'*. And some read ﴿wallāhu yurīdu al-ākhira﴾ ("Allah desires the Hereafter") with ﴿al-ākhira﴾ in the genitive case, by omitting the governing noun and leaving the noun in its governed form, as in the poet's words:

*Akullu imriʾin taḥsibīna imraʾan*
*wa-nārin tawaqqadu bi-l-layli nārā*

[This is from Abu Dawud. It is also said to be by Harithah ibn Hamran al-Iyadi, and it is among the verses of the Kitab (of Sibawayh). The hamza is an interrogative of disapproval, addressing a woman or himself: that is, do not suppose that every man is a complete man, and do not suppose that every fire that blazes at night is a blazing fire for entertaining guests. He means that the man is the generous and brave one, and the fire is only the fire of hospitality and nothing else. Omitting the governing noun while the governed noun remains in the genitive is regular when it is coordinated with a similar item so as to indicate it, as here; otherwise it is only transmitted, though it is regular according to the Kufans even without coordination. *Nār* is in the genitive governed by an omitted noun, and it cannot be coordinated with *imraʾ*. Coordinating an accusative with an accusative is to avoid coordinating upon the objects of two different governing words, namely *kull* and *taḥsibīna*, which Sibawayh and those who agree with him prohibit.]

Its meaning is "and Allah desires the Hereafter," in contrast, that is, its reward. ﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾: He overcomes His allies over their enemies and enables them to kill and capture them, and permits them ransom. ﴿But He is Wise﴾: He delays that until they become numerous and mighty, while they hasten.

﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that preceded﴾: had it not been a judgment from Him that had already been recorded in the Preserved Tablet, namely that He does not punish anyone for an error. This was an error in judgment, for they considered that sparing them might be a cause of their Islam and repentance, and that their ransom could strengthen them for jihad in the way of Allah. But it was hidden from them that killing them would strengthen Islam more, inspire awe in those behind them, and weaken their power. It was said: the decree was that He would make lawful for them the ransom they had taken. It was said: the people of Badr are forgiven. It was said: He does not punish a people except after the establishment of proof and the prior prohibition, and no prohibition had preceded regarding this.

﴿So eat of what you have taken as spoils﴾: it was narrated that they refrained from the spoils and did not reach out their hands to them, so this was revealed. It was said: it is a permission for the ransom, because it is among the spoils. ﴿And fear Allah﴾: so do not advance upon anything about which you have not been instructed.

Its meaning is: "We have now permitted you the spoils, so eat of what you have seized." As for His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, its meaning is that if you fear Him (ittaqaytumūhu) after what preceded from you in taking ransom (istibāḥat al-fidā') before permission was given to you for it, He will forgive you, show mercy to you, and turn toward you in repentance.

"And if they intend treachery against you, [then] they have already been treacherous toward Allah before, [so] He gave you power over them." Al-Zamakhshari: "If they intend treachery against you, that is, breaking what they pledged you of Islam, [returning to] apostasy, and preferring the religion of their fathers. ﴿Then they have already been treacherous toward Allah before﴾ in their disbelief in Him and their breaking of the covenant taken from every rational being. ﴿So He gave you power over them﴾, as you saw on the day of Badr. So He will give you power over them again if they repeat the treachery." And it has been said: the meaning of treachery here is withholding what they had guaranteed of ransom (fida').

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on Surah al-Anfal (8), verse 72:

"Those who emigrated" (alladhina hajaru): i.e., they left their homelands and their people out of love for Allah and His Messenger. These are the Muhajirun (the Emigrants). "And those who gave them refuge" (wa-alladhina awaw-hum) "and helped them" (wa-nasarohum) "against their enemies" (ila diyarihim wa-nasarohum 'ala a'da'ihim): these are the Ansar (the Helpers). "Some of them are allies of others" (ba'duhum awliya'u ba'd): i.e., some of them inherit from others. The Muhajirun and the Ansar used to inherit from one another by virtue of emigration and support, to the exclusion of blood relatives, until this was abrogated (naskh) by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And blood relatives are closer to one another﴾. It is also read "min wilayatihim" (from their allegiance), with fath and kasr, i.e., from their inheritance-right (tawalli) in the matter of inheritance. The reasoning for the kasr is that one party's taking charge of another is likened to a craft or profession, as if by taking charge of his companion he is engaged in an affair and undertaking a task. ﴿So upon you is support﴾: it is obligatory upon you to support them against the polytheists. ﴿Except against a people between you and them is a covenant﴾: it is not permissible for you to support them against those, because they do not initiate fighting, since the covenant prevents that.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 8, verse 73:

﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others.﴾ Its apparent meaning affirms wilaya (close allegiance and friendship) among them, like His saying, exalted is He, concerning the Muslims: ﴿Those are allies of one another.﴾ Its meaning is: He forbade the Muslims from taking as allies (muwalat) those who disbelieve, and from inheriting from them, and made it obligatory to keep away from them and sever relations with them, even if they are relatives, and that they should leave off inheriting from one another. Then He said:

﴿Unless you do it﴾, that is, unless you do what I have commanded you: the connection of the Muslims and the allegiance of some of them to others, even in inheritance, preferring the bond of Islam over the bond of kinship, and you do not cut the ties between you and the disbelievers.

﴿And you do not make their kinship into a kinship that exists, [and there will be] fitnah (turmoil) on the earth and great corruption,﴾ because, as long as the Muslims do not become one hand against polytheism (shirk), polytheism remains manifest and corruption increases. It is also read by Kathir with the letter thā' (ثاء).

Those are truly the believers. For they affirmed their faith and made it real by fulfilling its requirements: emigrating from their homeland, leaving their families, and parting with their wealth for the sake of the religion. This is not a repetition, because this verse comes to praise them and bear witness to them [[His words "and bearing witness to them" is perhaps: "and bearing witness to them of faith." (A.)]] together with the noble promise. The purpose of "and the ones who believed after this" is to mean those who came later, after the earlier ones to emigration, as in His words: ﴿And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith﴾. He joined them to those earlier believers and made them of their number, out of His grace and as an encouragement. "And those of kinship" means the blood relatives, or those more entitled to inheritance. This is an abrogation of inheritance through emigration and support. "In the Book of Allah" means in His judgment and His apportioning. It is said: in the Preserved Tablet. It is also said: in the Qur'an, namely the verses of inheritance. The companions of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, have used this verse as evidence for the inheritance of distant kin (dhawu al-arham).
